## Statement

Let $a<b$, $r\ge1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $g\in C^{r+1}[a,b]$ be real-valued with $|g'|\ge c>0$, and $h\in C^r[a,b]$ be complex-valued. With $T_g h=(h/g')'$ and $T_g^0h=h$ as in [[def-na-finite-interval-oscillatory-integral]], one has
$$I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b+\frac{(-1)^r}{(i\omega)^r}I_\omega(T_g^rh,g;[a,b]).$$
Consequently,
$$\left|I_\omega(h,g;[a,b])-\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jh(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b\right|\le\frac{b-a}{|\omega|^r}\|T_g^rh\|_\infty.$$
For fixed $h,g,r$, the remainder is $O(|\omega|^{-r})$; the constant is the displayed derivative norm, not a frequency-uniform assertion about varying $h$ or $g$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $a<b$, the hypotheses in the Statement, and the componentwise complex Riemann integral from [[def-na-finite-interval-oscillatory-integral]].

[F1] [[lem-na-complex-phase-derivative]]: $(e^{i\omega g})'=i\omega g'e^{i\omega g}$.

[F2] [[thm-integration-by-parts]]: for real $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on a closed interval, $\int u v'=[uv]-\int u'v$. Applying this to real and imaginary components gives the componentwise complex identity.

[F3] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, products, and quotients with nonzero denominator preserve differentiability and obey the stated derivative rules.

## Proof

1.1 Since $g'$ is continuous and nowhere zero, [F3] makes $h/g'$ differentiable with derivative $T_gh$. Apply [F2] componentwise with $u=h/g'$ and $v=e^{i\omega g}$. By [F1], $v'=i\omega g'v$, so rearranging gives $I_\omega(h,g)=[(h/g')v]_a^b/(i\omega)-I_\omega(T_gh,g)/(i\omega)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.1 successively to $h,T_gh,\ldots,T_g^{r-1}h$. At each application the final integral receives one further factor $-1/(i\omega)$ and the next endpoint term receives the matching alternating sign, yielding the displayed finite sum and remainder. Since $|e^{i\omega g(x)}|=1$, the remainder modulus is at most $|\omega|^{-r}\int_a^b|T_g^rh(x)|\,dx\le (b-a)|\omega|^{-r}\|T_g^rh\|_\infty$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $a<c<b$ and $f\in C^1([a,b])$, the principal value of [[def-cauchy-principal-value-subtraction]] exists and, with $g(c)=f'(c)$ and $g(x)=(f(x)-f(c))/(x-c)$ otherwise, satisfies
$$\operatorname{PV}\!\int_a^b\frac{f(x)}{x-c}\,dx=\int_a^b g(x)\,dx+f(c)\log\frac{b-c}{c-a}.$$
The first integral is an ordinary integral of a continuous function.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a<c<b$ and $f\in C^1([a,b])$.

[F1] [[def-cauchy-principal-value-subtraction]]: the principal value is the symmetric limit of the two truncated integrals.

[F2] [[lem-c1-divided-difference-extends-continuously]]: the subtraction quotient $g$ extended by $g(c)=f'(c)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: on $(0,\infty)$, $\log$ is a primitive of $1/x$ and is continuous; $\log u-\log v=\log(u/v)$ for $u,v>0$ ([[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]).

[F4] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: integrating a continuous derivative on a compact interval gives the endpoint difference.

[F5] [[thm-ftc-first-part]]: the integral function of a continuous integrand is a continuous primitive, so its increments over intervals whose endpoints tend to $c$ tend to zero.

## Proof

1.1 For $x\ne c$, $f(x)/(x-c)=g(x)+f(c)/(x-c)$. If $0<\varepsilon<\min(c-a,b-c)$, apply [F3]–[F4] separately on $[a,c-\varepsilon]$ and $[c+\varepsilon,b]$. The two singular terms sum to $$f(c)\bigl(\log\varepsilon-\log(c-a)+\log(b-c)-\log\varepsilon\bigr)=f(c)\log\frac{b-c}{c-a}.$$ Thus the truncated principal value equals $\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}g+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^b g+f(c)\log((b-c)/(c-a))$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Let $G(x)=\int_a^xg$. By [F2] and [F5], $G$ is continuous and its interval increments equal the corresponding integrals. Additivity gives $\int_a^{c-\varepsilon}g+\int_{c+\varepsilon}^b g=\int_a^b g-[G(c+\varepsilon)-G(c-\varepsilon)]$. The bracket tends to zero by continuity of $G$. [F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in step 1.1 and using step 2.1 proves existence of the symmetric limit and the asserted identity. Since $g$ is continuous, its ordinary integral exists. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

cases.review_reason: If the numerator value at the pole is zero, the logarithmic correction vanishes and the continuously extended divided difference supplies an ordinary integral.

The first integral is an ordinary integral of a continuous function.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a<c<b$ and $f\in C^1([a,b])$.

[F5] [[thm-ftc-first-part]]: the integral function of a continuous integrand is a continuous primitive, so its increments over intervals whose endpoints tend to $c$ tend to zero.

## Statement

Use one of the modes of [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]] and let $\Phi$ be its transformed real integrand. Suppose $\Phi$ has an extension $F$ satisfying all hypotheses of [[thm-analytic-strip-trapezoid-error]] for some $0<a<d$, with horizontal integrals $I_\pm=\int_{\mathbb R}|F(x\pm ia)|dx$. Also suppose $|\Phi(t)|\le A e^{-B e^{\kappa|t|}}$ for $|t|\ge T$, where $A,B,\kappa>0$, and $N_\pm h\ge T$. If $I$ is the target improper integral and $T_{h,N_-,N_+}$ is the finite sum in the algorithm, then it is absolutely convergent as an improper integral and
$$|I-T_{h,N_-,N_+}|\le\frac{I_++I_-}{e^{2\pi a/h}-1}+\frac{A}{\kappa B}\left(e^{-B e^{\kappa N_-h}}+e^{-B e^{\kappa N_+h}}\right).$$
The strip and tail hypotheses are separate assumptions; integrability alone implies neither estimate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A mode and transformed function $\Phi$ from [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]], its target $I$, an analytic extension satisfying the strip hypotheses, and a double-exponential real-tail envelope with the stated cutoff conditions.

[F1] [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]]: the output is $h\sum_{k=-N_-}^{N_+}\Phi(kh)$.

[F2] [[thm-double-exponential-transforms-and-integral-identities]]: if $\Phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, the target exists absolutely and equals $\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)dt$.

[F3] [[thm-analytic-strip-trapezoid-error]]: under the closed-substrip exponential bound and analyticity hypotheses, $\left|\int\Phi-h\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\Phi(kh)\right|\le(I_++I_-)/(e^{2\pi a/h}-1)$ and the infinite sum is absolutely convergent.

[F4] [[lem-double-exponential-truncated-tail-bound]]: the continuous and sampled omitted tails each have the stated one-sided envelope bound.

## Proof

1.1 Put $T_0=\max(T,0)$. The envelope holds for $|t|\ge T_0$, and $N_\pm h\ge0$ together with $N_\pm h\ge T$ gives $N_\pm h\ge T_0$. Thus [F4] applies with cutoff $T_0$ and makes $\Phi$ absolutely integrable outside $[-T_0,T_0]$. Continuity makes it bounded and integrable on $[-T_0,T_0]$, so $\Phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and [F2] identifies $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $h\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\Phi(kh)$ is absolutely convergent. Splitting its terms into $-N_-\le k\le N_+$ and the two omitted tails is therefore valid. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Add and subtract the infinite trapezoid sum. The triangle inequality bounds the target-to-finite-sum error by the target-to-infinite-sum error plus the absolute omitted sample sum. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the first term in step 2.1 and the sampled-tail estimate [F4], with cutoff $T_0$ from step 1.1, to the second. Their sum is the displayed bound. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

Use one of the modes of [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]] and let $\Phi$ be its transformed real integrand. Suppose $\Phi$ has an extension $F$ satisfying all hypotheses of [[thm-analytic-strip-trapezoid-error]] for some $0<a<d$, with horizontal integrals $I_\pm=\int_{\mathbb R}|F(x\pm ia)|dx$. Also suppose $|\Phi(t)|\le A e^{-B e^{\kappa|t|}}$ for $|t|\ge T$, where $A,B,\kappa>0$, and $N_\pm h\ge T$. If $I$ is the target improper integral and $T_{h,N_-,N_+}$ is the finite sum in the algorithm, then it is absolutely convergent as an improper integral and
$$|I-T_{h,N_-,N_+}|\le\frac{I_++I_-}{e^{2\pi a/h}-1}+\frac{A}{\kappa B}\left(e^{-B e^{\kappa N_-h}}+e^{-B e^{\kappa N_+h}}\right).$$
The strip and tail hypotheses are separate assumptions; integrability alone implies neither estimate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A mode and transformed function $\Phi$ from [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]], its target $I$, an analytic extension satisfying the strip hypotheses, and a double-exponential real-tail envelope with the stated cutoff conditions.

[F1] [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]]: the output is $h\sum_{k=-N_-}^{N_+}\Phi(kh)$.

[F2] [[thm-double-exponential-transforms-and-integral-identities]]: if $\Phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, the target exists absolutely and equals $\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)dt$.

[F3] [[thm-analytic-strip-trapezoid-error]]: under the closed-substrip exponential bound and analyticity hypotheses, $\left|\int\Phi-h\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\Phi(kh)\right|\le(I_++I_-)/(e^{2\pi a/h}-1)$ and the infinite sum is absolutely convergent.

[F4] [[lem-double-exponential-truncated-tail-bound]]: the continuous and sampled omitted tails each have the stated one-sided envelope bound.

## Proof

1.1 Put $T_0=\max(T,0)$. The envelope holds for $|t|\ge T_0$, and $N_\pm h\ge0$ together with $N_\pm h\ge T$ gives $N_\pm h\ge T_0$. Thus [F4] applies with cutoff $T_0$ and makes $\Phi$ absolutely integrable outside $[-T_0,T_0]$. Continuity makes it bounded and integrable on $[-T_0,T_0]$, so $\Phi\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and [F2] identifies $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $h\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\Phi(kh)$ is absolutely convergent. Splitting its terms into $-N_-\le k\le N_+$ and the two omitted tails is therefore valid. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Add and subtract the infinite trapezoid sum. The triangle inequality bounds the target-to-finite-sum error by the target-to-infinite-sum error plus the absolute omitted sample sum. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the first term in step 2.1 and the sampled-tail estimate [F4], with cutoff $T_0$ from step 1.1, to the second. Their sum is the displayed bound. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and put $V:=\operatorname{TV}(u_0)$.
Let $U^n=(U_j^n)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ be generated by
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]] under its full invariant-interval
CFL bound. Define the update map
$$H(a,b,c):=b-\lambda\bigl(F(b,c)-F(a,b)\bigr).$$
Then $H$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for
$s\in I$. Consequently,
$$a_-\le U_j^n\le a_+\quad(j\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge0),\qquad \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|\le V\quad(n\ge0).$$
Moreover, for every $n\ge0$,
$$\frac h\tau\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le (L_1+L_2)V.$$
For a sequence $x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$, the notation
$\|x\|_1:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}|x_j|$ is used only when this sum is finite;
$x\vee y$ and $x\wedge y$ mean the coordinatewise maximum and minimum.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $u_0$, $V$, the cells and cell-average initialization, a locally Lipschitz monotone consistent flux $F$ on $I=[a_-,a_+]$, coordinate bounds $L_1,L_2$, $\lambda=\tau/h$ with $\lambda(L_1+L_2)\le1$, and the flux-difference update.

[F1] $\operatorname{TV}(u_0)<\infty$ means $\int_{\mathbb R}|u_0(x+h)-u_0(x)|\,dx\le hV$ for every $h>0$ ([[def-bounded-bv-data-on-line]]).

[F2] Each updated coordinate is $H(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and $H$ is defined from the flux-difference rule ([[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]]).

## Proof

1.1 For a finite set $J\subset\mathbb Z$, the cell-average formula gives $\sum_{j\in J}|U_{j+1}^0-U_j^0|\le\frac1h\int_{\cup_{j\in J}I_j}|u_0(x+h)-u_0(x)|\,dx\le V.$ Taking the supremum over finite $J$ proves the initial discrete variation bound. Every initial cell average lies in $I$, since $a_-\le u_0\le a_+$ almost everywhere on its cell. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 If $a$ or $c$ increases, monotonicity of $F$ in its first or second coordinate makes $H$ nondecreasing in that variable. If $b_2\ge b_1$, coordinate Lipschitz bounds give $H(a,b_2,c)-H(a,b_1,c)\ge(b_2-b_1)\bigl(1-\lambda(L_1+L_2)\bigr)\ge0.$ Thus $H$ is nondecreasing in all coordinates. Consistency gives $H(s,s,s)=s$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $U^n$ takes values in $I$. Coordinatewise comparison with the constant triples $(a_-,a_-,a_-)$ and $(a_+,a_+,a_+)$, followed by step 1.2, yields $a_-=H(a_-,a_-,a_-)\le U_j^{n+1}\le H(a_+,a_+,a_+)=a_+$. Induction from step 1.1 proves the range bound at every time. [step 1.2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $S$ denote the sequence update. If $x,y\in I^{\mathbb Z}$ and $\sum_j|x_j-y_j|<\infty$, monotonicity gives $|Sx-Sy|\le S(x\vee y)-S(x\wedge y)$ coordinatewise. The difference on the right is summable: the update formula and the coordinate Lipschitz bounds make its flux differences summable. For any $z,w$ with $\sum_j|z_j-w_j|<\infty$, summing the update over $-N\le j\le N$ yields $\sum_{j=-N}^N(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_{j=-N}^N(z_j-w_j)-\lambda(d_N-d_{-N-1}),\quad d_j:=F(z_j,z_{j+1})-F(w_j,w_{j+1}).$ The coordinate Lipschitz bounds make $\sum_j|d_j|<\infty$, so both boundary terms tend to zero. The update difference is absolutely summable, and hence $\sum_j(Sz_j-Sw_j)=\sum_j(z_j-w_j)$. Applying this to $z=x\vee y$ and $w=x\wedge y$ proves $\|Sx-Sy\|_1\le\|x-y\|_1$. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The initial neighbor difference is summable by step 1.1. The update commutes with integer shifts because the same $H$ is applied at every index. Apply step 2.2 to $x=U^n$ and its shift $y_j=U_{j+1}^n$ to obtain $\sum_j|U_{j+1}^{n+1}-U_j^{n+1}|\le\sum_j|U_{j+1}^{n}-U_j^{n}|.$ Induction proves the stated TVD bound. [step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Adding and subtracting $F(U_j^n,U_j^n)$ in the update and using the two coordinate Lipschitz bounds gives $|U_j^{n+1}-U_j^n|\le\lambda\bigl(L_2|U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n|+L_1|U_j^n-U_{j-1}^n|\bigr).$ Multiply by $h/\tau=1/\lambda$, sum over $j$, and use step 3.1 to obtain the time-increment estimate. [F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, let $0<\lambda<\infty$, and let $u\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$. Since $D$ has finite measure, Hölder's inequality makes every $L^2(D)$ representative integrable, and almost-everywhere equal representatives have the same integral. Thus the local mean-zero space
$$Q_D:=\left\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\right\}.$$
Set $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$. Then $p\in Q_D$. If additionally $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $D$ is nonempty, connected, and Lipschitz, this $Q_D$ is exactly the space $Q=L^2_0(D)$ of [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], so $p$ belongs to the mixed elasticity model's pressure space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a bounded open $D$, a finite $\lambda>0$, $u\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, the local pressure space $Q_D$ in the Statement, and $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u$.

[A1] Countable Choice is required by the zero-mean-divergence supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] Every zero-boundary field has an $L^2$ divergence with integral zero. ([[lem-na-zero-mean-of-zero-boundary-divergence]])

[F2] On bounded $D$, every $L^2(D)$ representative is integrable by Hölder, the integral is unchanged under almost-everywhere equality, and it is linear; hence $Q_D=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}$ is a well-defined linear subspace. When $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $D$ is nonempty, bounded, connected, and Lipschitz, the imported Stokes definition uses exactly this $Q_D$. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]])

## Proof

1.1 Under [A1], [F1] gives $\operatorname{div}u\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}u=0$. By the definition of $Q_D$ in [F2], this means $\operatorname{div}u\in Q_D$. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Multiplication by the finite scalar $-\lambda$ preserves membership in the linear subspace $Q_D$. Therefore $p=-\lambda\operatorname{div}u\in Q_D$. In the stated connected Lipschitz model domain, [F2] identifies $Q_D$ with $Q$, giving the model-space conclusion as well. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

The SBP matrix identity alone guarantees that a naively collocated strong-form discretization of a nonlinear conservation law cannot increase its discrete quadratic entropy.

## Witness Data

Use one reference interval $[-1,1]$ with three Legendre–Gauss–Lobatto nodes $(-1,0,1)$, weights $H=\operatorname{diag}(1/3,4/3,1/3)$, derivative matrix
$$D=\begin{pmatrix}-3/2&2&-1/2\\-1/2&0&1/2\\1/2&-2&3/2\end{pmatrix},$$
and boundary matrix $B=\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,1)$. For periodic Burgers flux $f(u)=u^2/2$, define the naive collocated strong form
$$\dot U+D f(U)+H^{-1}B\bigl(\widehat f_{\partial}-f(U_{\partial})\bigr)=0,$$
where $\widehat f_{\partial}=(f(U_0)+f(U_2))/2$ is used at both periodic endpoints. Take $U=(-3,-1,-2)^T$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The three-node nodal vector, positive diagonal quadrature norm, exact SBP identity, pointwise Burgers flux, central periodic boundary flux, and quadratic entropy $E(U)=\frac12U^THU$.

[F1] [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]: SBP data satisfy $D\mathbf1=0$ and $HD+D^TH=B$ with positive diagonal $H$.

## Verification

1.1 Direct multiplication gives $D\mathbf1=0$ and $HD+D^TH=\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,1)=B$, so the derivative and norm satisfy the stated SBP identity. The three-point Gauss–Lobatto rule is exact through degree three, while both the quadratic entropy integrand $u_h^2$ and cubic entropy flux $u_h^3$ exceed that degree for a quadratic polynomial; the pointwise collocation therefore underintegrates these nonlinear products. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At the chosen state, $f(U)=(9/2,1/2,2)^T$ and $\widehat f_{\partial}=13/4$. Hence $Df(U)=(-27/4,-5/4,17/4)^T$ and $H^{-1}B(\widehat f_{\partial}-f(U_{\partial}))=(15/4,0,15/4)^T$. The semidiscrete residual is therefore $(-3,-5/4,8)^T$, so $\dot U=(3,5/4,-8)^T$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The discrete entropy rate is $\dot E=U^TH\dot U=(-3)(1/3)(3)+(-1)(4/3)(5/4)+(-2)(1/3)(-8)=2/3>0$. This exact periodic state contradicts the asserted universal nonincrease, despite the SBP identity; it does not contradict the entropy-stable flux-differencing theorem, which uses a different volume flux. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

At a face of the scheme in [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]], write $\alpha=a_R$ and $\beta=-a_L$. There are coefficients $p,q\ge0$ such that
$$\widehat F^h=p h_L^*-q h_R^*,\qquad p\le\alpha,\qquad q\le\beta.$$
If $\alpha>0$ and $h_L^*>0$, then $p<\alpha$; if $\beta>0$ and $h_R^*>0$, then $q<\beta$. These statements include the branches where one speed is zero and the all-dry branch.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hydrostatic reconstructed states, physical flux and HLL branch definitions. Derive the mass-flux coefficients and their bounds without assuming exact Riemann speeds.

[F1] [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]]: $\alpha=\max(0,u_L^*+c_L^*,u_R^*+c_R^*)$, $\beta=\max(0,c_L^*-u_L^*,c_R^*-u_R^*)$, and the middle mass flux is the first component of the displayed HLL formula.

[F2] [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]]: $F^h(U_s^*)=h_s^*u_s^*$, and $c_s^*=\sqrt{g h_s^*}$; when $h_s^*=0$, both $u_s^*$ and $F(U_s^*)$ are zero.

## Proof

1.1 In the middle branch $\alpha,\beta>0$. Define $p=\alpha(u_L^*+\beta)/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $q=\beta(\alpha-u_R^*)/(\alpha+\beta)$. Substituting $a_L=-\beta$ and $a_R=\alpha$ into [F1], then using [F2], gives $\widehat F^h=(\alpha h_L^*u_L^*+\beta h_R^*u_R^*-\alpha\beta(h_R^*-h_L^*))/(\alpha+\beta)=p h_L^*-q h_R^*$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The speed definitions give $u_L^*+\beta\ge c_L^*\ge0$, $\alpha-u_L^*\ge c_L^*\ge0$, $\alpha-u_R^*\ge c_R^*\ge0$, and $\beta+u_R^*\ge c_R^*\ge0$. Hence the coefficients in step 1.1 satisfy $p,q\ge0$, $p\le\alpha$, and $q\le\beta$. When $h_L^*>0$, $c_L^*>0$ and $\alpha-u_L^*>0$, so $p<\alpha$; when $h_R^*>0$, $c_R^*>0$ and $\beta+u_R^*>0$, so $q<\beta$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $a_L=0<a_R$, the first HLL branch gives $\widehat F^h=h_L^*u_L^*$; the speed definitions imply $u_L^*\ge c_L^*\ge0$ and $\alpha\ge u_L^*+c_L^*$, so take $p=u_L^*$ and $q=0$. If $a_L<0=a_R$, the second branch gives $\widehat F^h=h_R^*u_R^*$, with $u_R^*\le-c_R^*\le0$ and $\beta\ge c_R^*-u_R^*$, so take $p=0$ and $q=-u_R^*$. If both speeds vanish, their definitions force $u_s^*-c_s^*\ge0$ and $u_s^*+c_s^*\le0$ on each side, hence $c_s^*=u_s^*=h_s^*=0$ and the first branch returns zero. These choices satisfy the bounds in step 2.1 and cover every equality-speed branch. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take $\Omega=(0,2)\times(0,1)$ and the two rectangular cells $K=(0,1)\times(0,1)$ and $L=(1,2)\times(0,1)$. Their centers are $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(3/2,1/2)$, so the shared vertical face is orthogonal to the center segment. Set $\lambda_K=\lambda_L=1$, use $u(x,y)=x$, and impose its exact face-center values on the six cell faces on the outer boundary. The exact source is $f=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-cell mesh and data above, and the TPFA transmissibilities and signed fluxes from [[def-tpfa-harmonic-face-scheme]].

[F1] [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]]: $|K|=|L|=1$; the shared face has length $1$, and each outer face has length $1$.

[F2] [[def-tpfa-harmonic-face-scheme]]: $T_F=|F|/(d_{K,F}/\lambda_K+d_{L,F}/\lambda_L)$ on an interior face, and $T_{K,F}=|F|\lambda_K/d_{K,F}$ on a boundary face.

## Verification

1.1 The center-to-center distance across the shared face is $1$, with half-distances $d_{K,F}=d_{L,F}=1/2$. Thus $T_F=1$. The left and right boundary half-distances are $1/2$, so their transmissibilities are $2$; top and bottom center-to-face displacements are vertical and hence orthogonal to those faces. The mesh satisfies the TPFA orthogonality requirements. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The cell values are $u_K=1/2$ and $u_L=3/2$. At the shared face, $Q_{K,F}=1(1/2-3/2)=-1$ and $Q_{L,F}=1$. On the left boundary the outward flux is $2(1/2-0)=1$, and on the right boundary it is $2(3/2-2)=-1$. The top and bottom boundary fluxes vanish because their face-center values equal the adjacent cell-center values. Each cell balance therefore sums to zero, and the shared flux matches the exact outward diffusive flux $-\nabla u\cdot(1,0)=-1$ from $K$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite boundary-anchored cell-face mesh satisfy the face-moment closure in [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]], and let every $A_K$ be symmetric positive definite. Define
$$ \|v\|_{K,\mathrm{mim}}^2=|K||G_Kv|^2+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{|F|}{d_{K,F}}\rho_{K,F}(v)^2. $$
Then $\mathscr A_K(v,v)\ge\lambda_{\min}(A_K)\|v\|_{K,\mathrm{mim}}^2$. The global Dirichlet matrix of the linear hybrid mimetic scheme is symmetric positive definite and has a unique solution for every finite cell-source vector. Its induced numerical fluxes satisfy the cellwise balance and opposite-flux identity on each interior face. For any affine $\ell(x)=b\cdot x+c$, the local linear flux is exactly $Q_{K,F}(\ell)=-|F|(A_Kb)\cdot n_{K,F}$. For the nonlinear $p$-growth extension in [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]], the spatial operator is monotone and coercive in the reconstructed gradient and residual variables, and its shared interior face fluxes are conservative at each implicit time step.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite boundary-anchored cell-face mesh, cell and face centroid degrees of freedom, the face-moment closure, positive tensors $A_K$, and the linear hybrid mimetic scheme of [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]].

[F1] [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]]: cells and faces have positive finite measures, an interior face is shared by exactly two cells, and the cell graph is boundary anchored.

[F2] [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]]: $G_Kv=|K|^{-1}\sum_F|F|v_Fn_{K,F}$, $\rho_{K,F}(v)=v_F-v_K-G_Kv\cdot(x_F-x_K)$, and $\mathscr A_K$ is the sum of the tensor-gradient term and the nonnegative residual stabilization.

[A1] Each $A_K$ is symmetric positive definite, so $z\cdot A_Kz\ge\lambda_{\min}(A_K)|z|^2$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

[A2] In the nonlinear branch, $a(x,\xi)$ has the cellwise growth, coercivity, and monotonicity assumptions in [[def-hybrid-mimetic-fv-scheme]], with $p>1$ and $\alpha_{0,K}>0$.

## Proof

1.1 For an affine $\ell(x)=b\cdot x+c$, the cell and face means are $\ell_K=\ell(x_K)$ and $\ell_F=\ell(x_F)$. The first face-moment identity annihilates the constant term in $G_K\ell$; the transpose of the second identity is $\sum_F|F|n_{K,F}\otimes x_F=|K|I_d$, so $G_K\ell=b$. Hence $\rho_{K,F}(\ell)=\ell_F-\ell_K-b\cdot(x_F-x_K)=0$. [F2, given, algebra]

1.2 For arbitrary $v$, [A1] gives $|K|(A_KG_Kv)\cdot G_Kv\ge\lambda_{\min}(A_K)|K||G_Kv|^2$. The stabilization coefficient is $\lambda_{\min}(A_K)>0$, so summing its squared residual terms gives $\mathscr A_K(v,v)\ge\lambda_{\min}(A_K)\|v\|_{K,\mathrm{mim}}^2$. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.3 For the nonlinear flux, the cell average preserves monotonicity because $(b_K(\xi)-b_K(\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta)=\frac1{|K|}\int_K(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta)\,dx\ge0.$ The pointwise bounds in [A2] also give $b_K(\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-|K|^{-1}\int_Kh$ and $|b_K(\xi)|\le C(|K|^{-1}\int_Kg+|\xi|^{p-1})$. Thus the averaged flux retains monotonicity, coercivity, and $p$-growth. [A2, given, algebra]

2.1 The global form is symmetric because each $A_K$ is symmetric and the residual term is a symmetric product. If its energy at $v$ is zero, step 1.2 forces $G_Kv=0$ and every $\rho_{K,F}(v)=0$. The latter then gives $v_F=v_K$ on every face. Shared face values make all adjacent cell values equal, and a boundary face has prescribed value zero; boundary anchoring propagates this zero to every cell. Thus the homogeneous matrix has trivial kernel. It is square and finite-dimensional, so it is invertible and positive definite; every cell-source vector has a unique solution. [F1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 For an interior face $F=K|L$, the global equation tested by its shared face basis function gives $\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_{K,F})+\mathscr A_L(u,\phi_{L,F})=0$, hence $Q_{K,F}+Q_{L,F}=0$. For a cell basis $\phi_K$, the equation gives $\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_K)=\int_Kf$. The local constant vector $\mathbf1_K=\phi_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\phi_{K,F}$ has zero reconstructed gradient by the first face-moment identity and zero residual; therefore $\mathscr A_K(u,\mathbf1_K)=0$. Expanding this identity and using the cell equation yields $\sum_{F\subset\partial K}Q_{K,F}=\int_Kf$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.3 If $u$ is the face and cell averages of an affine $\ell$, step 1.1 gives $G_Ku=b$ and all residuals of $u$ vanish. For the local face basis, $G_K\phi_{K,F}=|F|n_{K,F}/|K|$. Thus $\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_{K,F})=|F|(A_Kb)\cdot n_{K,F}$, and the definition $Q_{K,F}=-\mathscr A_K(u,\phi_{K,F})$ gives the exact outward diffusive flux. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The scalar map $\psi_p(s)=|s|^{p-2}s$ is increasing: it is increasing on each half-line by monotonicity of $r\mapsto r^{p-1}$ for $r\ge0$, and its values are nonpositive on $s\le0$ and nonnegative on $s\ge0$. Hence $(\psi_p(r)-\psi_p(s))(r-s)\ge0$. For any two states $u,v$, the difference $\mathcal A_{h,K}(u;u-v)-\mathcal A_{h,K}(v;u-v)$ is the sum of $|K|(b_K(G_Ku)-b_K(G_Kv))\cdot(G_Ku-G_Kv)$ and the nonnegative residual terms $\alpha_{0,K}|F|d_{K,F}^{1-p}(\psi_p(\rho_{K,F}(u))-\psi_p(\rho_{K,F}(v)))(\rho_{K,F}(u)-\rho_{K,F}(v))$. Step 1.3 and scalar monotonicity make every term nonnegative. Testing with $v=u$ and using the coercivity bound in [A2] yields $\mathcal A_{h,K}(u;u)\ge |K|\left(\alpha|G_Ku|^p-|K|^{-1}\int_Kh\right)+\alpha_{0,K}\sum_F\frac{|F|}{d_{K,F}^{p-1}}|\rho_{K,F}(u)|^p.$ For a fixed state, the local constant test vector has zero gradient and residual, so the spatial form annihilates it. A shared interior-face test in an implicit step makes $Q_{K,F}^{\rm nl}+Q_{L,F}^{\rm nl}=0$. Testing the step equation by the cell basis gives $\mathcal A_{h,K}(u^n;\phi_K)=|K|f_K^n-|K|(u_K^n-u_K^{n-1})/\tau_n$. Expanding the zero constant-test identity gives $\sum_FQ_{K,F}^{\rm nl}=|K|f_K^n-|K|(u_K^n-u_K^{n-1})/\tau_n$, the local balance with accumulation. [A2, F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proposition proves local coercivity in the explicitly defined gradient-residual norm and affine flux exactness. It does not assert a discrete maximum principle for the mimetic scheme or a mesh-uniform condition number without additional mesh-family estimates.

For any affine $\ell(x)=b\cdot x+c$, the local linear flux is exactly $Q_{K,F}(\ell)=-|F|(A_Kb)\cdot n_{K,F}$. ## Statement

For the scaled kernels of [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]] and every ε>0, supp W_ε⊂\overline B(0,Rε), ∫W_ε=1, ∫zW_ε(z)dz=0, and ∫|z|²W_ε(z)dz=ε²m₂. Pointwise, ∇W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−1)∇W(z/ε) and D²W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−2)D²W(z/ε); consequently their sup norms equal ε^(−d−1)M₁ and ε^(−d−2)M₂.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The admissible kernel W and a scale ε>0.

[F1] [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]]: W_ε(z)=ε^(−d)W(z/ε), supp W⊂\overline B(0,R), and the constants M₁, M₂, m₂ are finite.

[F2] [[lem-symmetric-kernel-moment-cancellation]]: ∫zW(z)dz=0.

[F3] [[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]]: if T:U→V is injective C¹ with invertible derivative and f is compactly supported Riemann integrable with support in V, then ∫_Vf(y)dy=∫_Uf(T(x))|det DT(x)|dx.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]: continuous real integrands on compact Jordan boxes are Riemann integrable.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of compositions with the affine scaling map are given by the chain rule.

## Proof

1.1 If W_ε(z)≠0 then z/ε∈supp W, so |z|≤Rε. The chain rule in [F5] applied to ε^(−d)W(z/ε) gives the displayed pointwise first and second derivative formulas; taking suprema and substituting u=z/ε gives the claimed derivative sup norms. [F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The functions W_ε, zW_ε, and |z|²W_ε are continuous and compactly supported, hence integrable on a bounding box by [F4]. In the integrals, the affine substitution z=εu has Jacobian determinant ε^d. Thus ∫W_ε=∫W=1, ∫zW_ε(z)dz=ε∫uW(u)du=0 by [F2], and ∫|z|²W_ε(z)dz=ε²∫|u|²W(u)du=ε²m₂. [F1, F2, F3, F4] ∎

## Statement

For the scaled kernels of [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]] and every ε>0, supp W_ε⊂\overline B(0,Rε), ∫W_ε=1, ∫zW_ε(z)dz=0, and ∫|z|²W_ε(z)dz=ε²m₂. Pointwise, ∇W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−1)∇W(z/ε) and D²W_ε(z)=ε^(−d−2)D²W(z/ε); consequently their sup norms equal ε^(−d−1)M₁ and ε^(−d−2)M₂.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The admissible kernel W and a scale ε>0.

[F1] [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]]: W_ε(z)=ε^(−d)W(z/ε), supp W⊂\overline B(0,R), and the constants M₁, M₂, m₂ are finite.

[F2] [[lem-symmetric-kernel-moment-cancellation]]: ∫zW(z)dz=0.

[F3] [[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]]: if T:U→V is injective C¹ with invertible derivative and f is compactly supported Riemann integrable with support in V, then ∫_Vf(y)dy=∫_Uf(T(x))|det DT(x)|dx.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]: continuous real integrands on compact Jordan boxes are Riemann integrable.

[F5] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: derivatives of compositions with the affine scaling map are given by the chain rule.

2.1 The functions W_ε, zW_ε, and |z|²W_ε are continuous and compactly supported, hence integrable on a bounding box by [F4]. In the integrals, the affine substitution z=εu has Jacobian determinant ε^d. Thus ∫W_ε=∫W=1, ∫zW_ε(z)dz=ε∫uW(u)du=0 by [F2], and ∫|z|²W_ε(z)dz=ε²∫|u|²W(u)du=ε²m₂. [F1, F2, F3, F4] ∎

## Definition

Fix $d\ge1$, $N\ge2$, $h=1/N$, $\nu>0$, $k>0$, and a step $n\ge1$. Supply
$u^{n-1},u^n\in V_h$ with zero discrete divergence, a mean-zero
$p^n\in Q_h$, and $f^{n+1}\in V_h$ whose components each have zero discrete
mean,
$$h^d\sum_{j\in J_N}f_{i,j}^{n+1}=0\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$
Compute a predictor
$\widetilde u^{n+1}\in V_h$ from
$$ \frac{3\widetilde u^{n+1}-4u^n+u^{n-1}}{2k} +\nu A_h\widetilde u^{n+1}+G_hp^n=f^{n+1}, $$
then solve for the unique mean-zero $\phi^{n+1}\in Q_h$ from
$$ \Delta_h\phi^{n+1}=\frac{3}{2k}D_h\widetilde u^{n+1}. $$
Set $u^{n+1}=\widetilde u^{n+1}-(2k/3)G_h\phi^{n+1}$. Choose exactly one
pressure update:

- **Standard incremental:** $p^{n+1}=p^n+\phi^{n+1}$.
- **Rotational incremental:** $p^{n+1}=p^n+\phi^{n+1}-\nu D_h\widetilde u^{n+1}$.

In both branches the pressure is gauged in $Q_h$. Initial values $u^0,u^1,p^1$
are supplied by the caller; no initialization accuracy, stability, or
convergence rate is asserted here. The separate well-definedness theorem
[[thm-na-periodic-pressure-correction-solves-well-defined]] verifies the
predictor and pressure solves for either branch.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge2$, $1/2<s\le1$, and a shape-regular affine simplicial mesh family as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. For $0<s<1$ and a scalar or vector-valued function $w$ on a cell $K$, define
$$|w|_{s,K}^2:=\int_K\int_K\frac{|w(x)-w(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dx\,dy;$$
for $s=1$ set $|w|_{1,K}:=\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}$ (componentwise for vectors). For every cell $K$, facet $F\subset\partial K$, and $w\in H^s(K)$ in the restriction convention of [[def-nitsche-restriction-bessel-potential-sobolev-spaces]], the trace from [[lem-nitsche-fractional-face-trace-on-simplex]] satisfies
$$\|T_Fw\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C\bigl(h_K^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2+h_K^{2s-1}|w|_{s,K}^2\bigr).$$
For $0<s<1$, the norm $\bigl(\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2+|w|_{s,K}^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ is equivalent on a fixed reference simplex to the restriction $H^s$ norm. At $s=1$ the displayed estimate is the weak $H^1$ trace inequality; no additional identification of the full intrinsic weak-$H^1$ space with a restriction space is asserted. Constants are uniform over the shape-regular family and depend only on $d,s$ and its shape bound.

For every $w\in H^s(K)$, with cell mean $w_K:=|K|^{-1}\int_Kw$, the same conventions give
$$\|w-w_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^s|w|_{s,K}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a fixed $d\ge2$; $1/2<s\le1$; a shape-regular affine simplex $K$ and facet $F$; the restriction Bessel-potential convention; and the $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform.

[F1] Whole-space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ is the Bessel-potential completion with norm $\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\widehat U\|_2$, its Fourier characterization is exact, and Fourier transformation is unitary on $L^2$ ([[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-fractional-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]], [[thm-plancherel]]).

[F2] The restriction space on an open set has the infimum extension norm; the existing simplex trace is the unique restriction of the whole-space hyperplane trace and is bounded for every exponent greater than $1/2$ ([[def-nitsche-restriction-bessel-potential-sobolev-spaces]], [[lem-nitsche-fractional-face-trace-on-simplex]]).

[F3] For a shape-regular affine map from the reference simplex, its singular values are comparable to $h_K$, its determinant to $h_K^d$, and each facet surface Jacobian to $h_K^{d-1}$ ([[lem-shape-regular-affine-simplex-scaling]]).

[F4] On the reference simplex, smooth functions on a neighbourhood of the closure are dense in $W^{1,2}$ and restriction to a facet extends boundedly to $L^2$ ([[lem-smooth-density-on-reference-simplex]], [[thm-reference-simplex-trace-and-gauss-green]]). The mean-zero $W^{1,2}$ Poincaré inequality holds there ([[thm-reference-simplex-poincare-wirtinger]]).

[F5] Smooth cutoffs with prescribed compact support exist. A nonnegative smooth bump that is one on a ball and supported in a larger ball can be normalized to give a compactly supported smooth unit-mass mollifier; its convolution is smooth. Translations are continuous in finite $L^2$ (also on $\mathbb R^{2d}$), and $L^2$ is complete ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]], [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]], [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]], [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]], [[thm-translation-is-continuous-in-l-p-for-one-le-p-less-infinity]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]).

[F6] Tonelli/Fubini and Jensen's inequality apply to the nonnegative integrands and probability averages below. The change-of-variables formula for nonnegative Lebesgue integrands applies to each invertible affine map on the open sets where it is used, including translations, products of affine maps, and the affine pieces of the reflection in step 2.2; in particular it gives $\int\rho_\varepsilon=1$ for the rescaled unit-mass mollifier. ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]], [[thm-jensens-integral-inequality]], [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]). ## Proof


**Given:** The hypotheses and [F1]–[F6].

1.1 For $U\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ and $0<s<1$, the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,z=y-x)$ is an invertible linear $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^{2d}$ with determinant of absolute value $1$. Apply the change-of-variables formula in [F6] to the nonnegative integrand, then Tonelli and Plancherel in the $x$ variable, to obtain $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|U(x)-U(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+2s}}\,dx\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\widehat U(\xi)|^2\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{|e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot z}-1|^2}{|z|^{d+2s}}\,dz\right)d\xi=c_{d,s}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\xi|^{2s}|\widehat U(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.$ The inner integral is finite because its numerator is at most $C|z|^2$ near zero and at most $4$ at infinity, giving radial integrals $\int_0^1r^{1-2s}dr$ and $\int_1^\infty r^{-1-2s}dr$; it is positive for $\xi\ne0$. Rotation and dilation, each covered by [F6], give the factor $c_{d,s}|\xi|^{2s}$. The vector-valued version follows by applying this identity to each component and summing. Since $1+|\xi|^{2s}$ is comparable to $\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}$, this identifies the whole-space intrinsic norm with the Bessel norm on Schwartz functions. [A1, F1, F6, given]

1.2 We construct finitely many boundary charts. At each boundary point choose an inward direction in the interior cone of the simplex; in a sufficiently small rotated box the active facet inequalities solve for the vertical coordinate and give $t>g(x')$, where $g$ is the maximum of finitely many affine functions. Inactive facets stay away after shrinking the box. If the affine functions are $\ell_j$, then $|g(x')-g(y')|\le L|x'-y'|$ with $L:=\max_j|\nabla\ell_j|$, so $g$ is Lipschitz in this explicit sense. Compactness gives a finite cover of the boundary by smaller such boxes and one interior open set covering the remaining compact subset. Choose nonnegative smooth cutoffs $\eta_j$ supported in the corresponding larger chart sets and positive on the smaller cover. Their sum is positive on a neighborhood of the closed simplex, so $\psi_j:=\eta_j/(\sum_i\eta_i)$ there form a smooth finite partition of unity. Multiplication by each cutoff is bounded in the intrinsic norm: expand $\chi(x)w(x)-\chi(y)w(y)$ into $\chi(x)(w(x)-w(y))+w(y)(\chi(x)-\chi(y))$; the second term is bounded by $C\|w\|_2^2$ because $|\chi(x)-\chi(y)|\le\min(C|x-y|,2\|\chi\|_\infty)$ and the resulting radial kernel is integrable for $0<s<1$. [F5, F6, given]

2.1 The identity extends to the completion, and that completion is exactly the $L^2$ functions with finite displayed intrinsic seminorm. For the converse density, choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_R$ equal to one on $B_R$, supported in $B_{2R}$, with $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. For any such function $W$, the difference quotient of $(1-\chi_R)W$ is the sum of $(1-\chi_R(x))(W(x)-W(y))$ and $W(y)(\chi_R(y)-\chi_R(x))$. Dominated convergence sends the first term to zero in the weighted pair $L^2$ norm; for the second, integration in $x-y$ gives at most $C R^{-2s}\|W\|_2^2$. Thus $\chi_RW\to W$ in the intrinsic norm. For compactly supported $W$, translation is continuous in $L^2$ both for $W$ and for $G_W(x,y):=(W(x)-W(y))/|x-y|^{d/2+s}$ under the simultaneous translation $(x,y)\mapsto(x-a,y-a)$. Choose a nonnegative smooth compactly supported unit-mass mollifier $\rho$. For a scalar function $Z$ and probability density $\rho_\varepsilon$, scalar Jensen gives $|\int \rho_\varepsilon(a)Z(a)\,da|^2\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)|Z(a)|^2\,da$. For a finite-dimensional Euclidean-valued $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$, apply this to each real component and sum: $|\int \rho_\varepsilon Z|^2=\sum_{j=1}^m|\int\rho_\varepsilon Z_j|^2\le\sum_{j=1}^m\int\rho_\varepsilon|Z_j|^2=\int\rho_\varepsilon|Z|^2$. Applying this inequality to the scalar or vector differences for $W$ and $G_W$, then Tonelli, gives $\|\rho_\varepsilon*W-W\|_2^2+[\rho_\varepsilon*W-W]_{s,\mathbb R^d}^2\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)\bigl(\|W(\cdot-a)-W\|_2^2+\|G_W(\cdot-a,\cdot-a)-G_W\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})}^2\bigr)\,da.$ The right side tends to zero because both translation differences tend to zero as $a\to0$ and the mollifier supports shrink to zero. The convolution is smooth by [F5], so $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Conversely, an intrinsic-Cauchy smooth sequence has an $L^2$ limit and a weighted-pair-$L^2$ limit; an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence identifies the latter with the difference quotient of the former. Completeness and [F1] therefore identify the completion with the intrinsic space. [A1, F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a boundary-localized piece, reflect across its graph by $R(x',t)=(x',2g(x')-t)$ and set the extension below the graph to $w(R(x',t))$. The horizontal coordinates are unchanged and the vertical difference is bounded by $|t-u|+2L|x'-y'|$, so $|Rx-Ry|\le C|x-y|$; since $R^2$ is the identity, the reverse bound follows by applying the same estimate to $Rx,Ry$. Thus $R$ is bi-Lipschitz. Because $g$ is a finite maximum of affine functions, partition each integration region into the finitely many open affine pieces; their boundaries lie in finitely many hyperplanes and are null. On each piece $R$ is an affine $C^1$ diffeomorphism with determinant of absolute value $1$. Apply the nonnegative change-of-variables formula in [F6] on each such piece (and in the $y$ variable for the mixed term); Tonelli combines the resulting estimates. Consequently same-side double integrals are bounded by a constant multiple of the upper-side integral. For $x$ above and $y$ below the graph, write their heights above the graph as $a,b\ge0$. Then $a+b\le|x_d-y_d|+L|x'-y'|$, hence $|x-Ry|\le C|x-y|$; the same piecewise affine changes of variables $y\mapsto Ry$ bound the mixed integral by the upper-side seminorm. Choose chart supports with positive margin to the artificial box edges, so cross pairs for extension by zero contribute at most $C\|w\|_2^2$; the interior piece has positive distance from the simplex boundary and obeys the same bound. Sum the finitely many extensions of $\psi_jw$. The result equals $w$ on the reference simplex and is bounded in intrinsic norm. [F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Restricting any whole-space extension decreases both the $L^2$ norm and the nonnegative pair integral. Conversely, step 2.2 supplies a bounded extension of every intrinsic reference-simplex function; together with step 2.1 this proves equivalence of the intrinsic and restriction $H^s$ norms for $0<s<1$. Apply the whole-space Fourier hyperplane trace bound [F2] to that extension; restriction to the reference facet gives its trace, and uniqueness in [F2] identifies it with the existing trace. At $s=1$, [F4] gives on the reference simplex $\|Tw\|_F^2\le C(\|w\|_K^2+\|\nabla w\|_K^2)$ for weak $H^1$ functions; density identifies it with the restriction trace whenever the input has a whole-space extension. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Pull back by the shape-regular affine map. The map from the reference open simplex to the cell interior and its product map on the double integral are invertible affine $C^1$ diffeomorphisms. Apply the nonnegative formula in [F6] to the $L^2$ and pair-integral terms; the determinant and singular-value bounds in [F3] show that for $0<s<1$ the $L^2$ term on the reference simplex is bounded by $C h_K^{-d}\|w\|_K^2$, and its pair seminorm by $C h_K^{2s-d}|w|_{s,K}^2$: the two volume Jacobians contribute $h_K^{-2d}$ and the inverse-map distance contributes at most $C h_K^{d+2s}$. Multiplying the reference trace bound by the facet Jacobian $C h_K^{d-1}$ yields the asserted terms $h_K^{-1}\|w\|_K^2$ and $h_K^{2s-1}|w|_{s,K}^2$. At $s=1$, write $\widehat w=w\circ F_K$, where $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$. The affine weak-derivative pullback used by the scaling supplier [F3] gives $\nabla_{\widehat x}\widehat w=A_K^T(\nabla w)\circ F_K$. Together with [F6], its full volume-scaled norm bound is $\|\nabla_{\widehat x}\widehat w\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}\le\|A_K\|\,|\det A_K|^{-1/2}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{1-d/2}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}$, while $\|\widehat w\|_{L^2(\widehat K)}^2=|\det A_K|^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2$. Multiply the squared reference trace inequality of step 3.1 by the facet surface Jacobian $J_F\le C h_K^{d-1}$ from [F3]. This gives $\|T_Fw\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C J_F|\det A_K|^{-1}\bigl(\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\|A_K\|^2\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}^2\bigr)\le C\bigl(h_K^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K)}^2+h_K\|\nabla w\|_{L^2(K)}^2\bigr)$. The same calculation applies componentwise to vector fields and the squared component norms add. [F3, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

The scaled estimate is proved here from the whole-space Fourier trace inequality and an explicit fractional-norm reflection extension on a simplex. The $s=1$ endpoint uses the published reference-simplex density and trace results. The argument does not use a $C^1$-boundary trace theorem, and the intrinsic weak-$H^1$ space is not identified with the restriction space.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let the mesh, coefficients, and SIPDG form be as in [[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]]. Suppose $u|_K\in H^2(K)$ on every cell, its facet traces agree across every interior facet, its boundary trace is zero, and $f|_K=-\nabla\cdot(A_K\nabla u)$ on each cell with $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. Assume also that the normal coefficient fluxes agree across interior facets: $(A_{K^-}\nabla u^- )\cdot n_F=(A_{K^+}\nabla u^+ )\cdot n_F$. Then for every $w_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$,
$$a_h(u,w_h)=\ell_h(w_h):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K f w_h\,dx.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; a finite matching affine simplicial mesh; cellwise constant symmetric positive-definite $A_K$; a piecewise $H^2$ function $u$ with matching interior traces and zero boundary trace; a piecewise $L^2$ source $f=-\nabla\cdot(A_K\nabla u)$; and matching interior normal fluxes.

[F1] The SIPDG form contains the broken volume term, the two symmetric flux-jump terms, and the jump penalty; the boundary jump equals the trace of its cell. ([[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]], [[def-sipdg-jump-average-convention]])

[F2] On each physical affine simplex, for scalar $v\in W^{1,2}$ and vector field $G\in W^{1,2}$, the transferred face traces satisfy $\int_Kv\,\operatorname{div}G+\nabla v\cdot G=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\gamma_Fv)(\gamma_FG)\cdot n_{K,F}$. ([[lem-sipdg-physical-simplex-trace-green]])

[F3] Countable Choice is the stated hypothesis of the physical-simplex trace and Green identity [F2]. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F4] $H^2(K)$ means $W^{2,2}(K)$ and $W^{1,2}(K)$ consists of $L^2$ classes with first weak derivatives in $L^2$. ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]])

## Proof

1.1 On each cell $K$, take $v=w_h|_K$ and $G=A_K\nabla u$. Since $u|_K\in H^2(K)$, [F4] and constant $A_K$ give $G\in W^{1,2}(K;\mathbb R^d)$, so [F2] and the cell equation yield $\int_KA_K\nabla u\cdot\nabla w_h=\int_Kfw_h+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(A_K\nabla u\cdot n_{K,F})w_h|_K$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Sum step 1.1 over cells. On an interior facet the two outward normals are $n_F$ and $-n_F$; the assumed normal-flux equality makes the two boundary terms equal $\int_Fq_F(u)[w_h]_F$. On a boundary facet the single term is also $\int_Fq_F(u)[w_h]_F$ by the one-sided convention. Therefore the broken volume term equals $\ell_h(w_h)+\sum_F\int_Fq_F(u)[w_h]_F$. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The matching traces of $u$ and its zero boundary trace give $[u]_F=0$ on every facet. Substitution into the SIPDG form makes its second flux-jump term exactly cancel the face sum of step 2.1, while its adjoint-consistency term and penalty term vanish. Hence $a_h(u,w_h)=\ell_h(w_h)$. [F1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega=(-1,1)^2$ be covered by a finite matching cell mesh, and let $\Phi,\Phi_h$ be continuous geometry maps whose cellwise $C^1$ derivatives satisfy $\|D\Phi\|_\infty+\|D\Phi_h\|_\infty\le M$, $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_\infty$, and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty;op}$. Let $G$ be a scalar physical boundary lift on an open convex neighborhood containing both images and every segment joining corresponding image points, with $\|DG\|_\infty\le L_1$ and $\|D^2G\|_\infty\le L_2$. Define the piecewise pullback gradients by $\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T\nabla G(\Phi)$ and $\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)=D\Phi_h^T\nabla G(\Phi_h)$, and set
$$\ell_{\partial,h}(w)=\int_{\widehat\Omega}\big(\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)\big)\cdot\nabla w,\qquad w\in H^1_0(\widehat\Omega).$$
With the $H^1$ dual norm, $\|\ell_{\partial,h}\|_{(H^1_0)^*}\le 2(L_1e_1+ML_2e_0)$. Thus the geometry-induced boundary-lift contribution to the Strang load defect is $O(e_0+e_1)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the reference square; continuous, cellwise $C^1$ maps with the stated derivative gap and upper bound; a $C^2$ lift $G$ on a convex neighborhood of both images; and $w\in H^1_0(\widehat\Omega)$.

[F1] [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]]: $e_0$ and $e_1$ are the uniform value and derivative gaps between exact and approximate geometry maps.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: $D(G\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T(DG\circ\Phi)$ wherever the cell maps are differentiable.

[F3] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: $|\int f\cdot g|\le\|f\|_{L^2}\|g\|_{L^2}$.

[F4] Under Countable Choice, the Lebesgue measurable sets form a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set, and Lebesgue measure agrees there with elementary volume. For the half-open box $B=[-1,1)^2$, its elementary volume is $4$.
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]],
[[thm-elementary-volume-is-well-defined]],
[[def-half-open-box]],
[[def-elementary-set-in-rn]])

[F5] A measure is nonnegative and finitely additive on disjoint measurable sets; consequently it is monotone on measurable sets, since $E\subseteq B$ gives $B=E\cup(B\setminus E)$.
([[def-measure]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed exactly for [F4] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Because each geometry map and its traces are continuous across every interior facet, $G\circ\Phi$ and $G\circ\Phi_h$ have matching traces there. For a compactly supported smooth test function, integration by parts cell by cell cancels the interior-facet terms; the outer boundary term vanishes because the test is compactly supported. Thus the displayed piecewise gradients are the weak gradients of the pulled-back lifts. On each cell, [F2] and the triangle inequality give $|\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)|\le L_1e_1+ML_2e_0,$ using the bound on $D^2G$ along the joining segment. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For $n\ge2$ put $B_n=[-1+1/n,1-1/n)^2$. Each $B_n$ is an elementary half-open box, and $(-1,1)^2=\bigcup_{n\ge2}B_n$: one inclusion is immediate, and for any $x\in(-1,1)^2$ choose $n$ with $1/n<\min_i\{1+x_i,1-x_i\}$ for both coordinates. Thus [F4] makes $\widehat\Omega$ measurable. Since $\widehat\Omega\subset B=[-1,1)^2$, [F5] and [F4] give $|\widehat\Omega|\le\lambda_2(B)=4$. Step 1.1 therefore yields $\|\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)}\le 2(L_1e_1+ML_2e_0).$ [F4, F5, A1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the defining integral for $\ell_{\partial,h}(w)$ and use $\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}\le\|w\|_{H^1}$. Taking the supremum over unit $H^1_0$ tests proves the dual bound. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega$ be bounded, let $\Phi,\Phi_h$ be the geometry maps of [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]] and assume each is a global orientation-preserving $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $\widehat\Omega$ onto its image, with $J_h\le J^*$ and $u$ is $L_u$-Lipschitz on the union of their images. On $\Omega_h=\Phi_h(\widehat\Omega)$ let $\mathcal S=(S_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j=1}^n$ be finite families of Lebesgue-measurable sets of positive measure satisfying
$$|\Omega_h\setminus\textstyle\bigcup_i S_i|=|\Omega_h\setminus\textstyle\bigcup_j T_j|=0,\qquad |S_i\cap S_{i'}|=0\ (i\ne i'),\qquad |T_j\cap T_{j'}|=0\ (j\ne j').$$
Thus each family is a finite measurable partition up to null sets as required by [[def-intersection-volume-conservative-remapping]]. Let $v_S$ be source-piecewise-constant data with finite $L^2$ error. Assume the exact target projection error below is finite. Define $P_Tq$ on each target cell by its exact cell average, $\eta_S=\|u-v_S\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}$, and $\eta_T=\|u-P_Tu\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}$. If $R$ is the exact overlap remap, then\n$$\|u\circ\Phi-(Rv_S)\circ\Phi_h\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega,J_h)}\le L_u e_0\sqrt{J^*|\widehat\Omega|}+\eta_S+\eta_T,$$\nwhere $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_\infty$ and $\|z\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega,J_h)}^2=\int_{\widehat\Omega}|z|^2J_h$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the exact and approximate maps; a bounded approximate Jacobian; a Lipschitz field on both images; two finite measurable families satisfying the displayed coverage and pairwise-null-overlap conditions; and source values constant on source cells.

[F1] [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]]: $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_\infty$ and $J_h$ is the positive approximate Jacobian.

[F2] [[def-intersection-volume-conservative-remapping]] and [[thm-overlap-remap-l2-projection-conservation-positivity]]: exact overlap remapping of source constants is the target-cell average projection.

[F3] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: $|\int_Tq|^2\le |T|\int_T|q|^2$ on every finite-volume target cell.

[F4] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism transforms nonnegative integrals by its positive Jacobian.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed exactly for [F4] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 The Lipschitz condition gives $|u(\Phi(X))-u(\Phi_h(X))|\le L_ue_0$ for every $X$. Integrating its square against $J_h\le J^*$ gives the geometry term $L_ue_0\sqrt{J^*|\widehat\Omega|}$. [F1, given]

1.2 For any $q\in L^2(\Omega_h)$ and target cell $T$, [F3] gives $|T||P_Tq|_T^2=|\int_Tq|^2/|T|\le\int_T|q|^2$. Summing over the disjoint target cells shows $P_T$ is contractive. The same averaging identity gives $q-P_Tq$ orthogonal to every target-cellwise constant, so $P_T$ is the orthogonal projection. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $Rv_S=P_Tv_S$. Thus $u-Rv_S=(u-P_Tu)+P_T(u-v_S)$; the two terms are orthogonal and $P_T$ is contractive by step 1.2. The first term has norm $\eta_T$ and the second is at most $\eta_S$, whence $\|u-Rv_S\|_{L^2(\Omega_h)}\le\eta_T+\eta_S$. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F4] separately on the finitely many mesh cells to identify the physical $L^2(\Omega_h)$ norm in step 2.1 with the weighted pullback norm of $(u-Rv_S)\circ\Phi_h$. The triangle inequality with step 1.1 proves the claimed bound. [F4, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For integers $\ell\ge0$ and real $z>0$, write $h_\ell=h_\ell^{(1)}$ using [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]]. Then
$$|h_\ell(z)|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}S_{\ell m}z^{-2m-2},\qquad S_{\ell m}=\frac{(2m)!(\ell+m)!}{4^m(m!)^2(\ell-m)!}.$$
Consequently $|h_\ell(z)|$ is nonincreasing in $z$, $|h_{\ell-1}(z)|\le|h_\ell(z)|$ for $\ell\ge1$, and $|h_\ell'(z)|\le(1+(\ell+1)/z)|h_\ell(z)|$. For every fixed $z_0>0$ and all $z\ge z_0$,
$$\frac{|z(h_\ell'(z)-ih_\ell(z))|}{|h_\ell(z_0)|}\le(\ell+1)e^{2z_0}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-derivative outgoing Hankel convention and its radial recurrences.

[F1] [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]]: $h_\ell=(-z)^\ell(z^{-1}d/dz)^\ell(-ie^{iz}/z)$.

[F2] [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]]: $h_{\ell+1}=\ell h_\ell/z-h_\ell'$ and $h_\ell'=h_{\ell-1}-(\ell+1)h_\ell/z$ for $\ell\ge1$.

## Proof

**Given:** Integer $\ell\ge0$, real $z>0$, and [F1]–[F2].

1.1 Direct differentiation of $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$ gives the finite expression $h_\ell(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}e^{iz}\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}i^m A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1},\qquad A_{\ell m}=\frac{(\ell+m)!}{m!(\ell-m)!2^m}.$ Indeed it holds at $\ell=0$; substituting this expression in $h_{\ell+1}=\ell h_\ell/z-h_\ell'$ gives $A_{\ell+1,m}=A_{\ell m}+(\ell+m)A_{\ell,m-1}$ (out-of-range coefficients are zero), and the displayed factorial formula satisfies that recurrence and the $m=0$ base. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $F_\ell=|h_\ell|^2$. The radial recurrence gives $h_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)h_\ell/z-h_{\ell-1}$. Also $F_\ell'=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar h_\ell h_{\ell-1})-2(\ell+1)F_\ell/z$ by [F2]. Expanding the squared modulus and eliminating the real cross term yields $F_{\ell+1}=F_{\ell-1}-(2\ell+1)F_\ell'/z-(2\ell+1)F_\ell/z^2.$ From $F_0=z^{-2}$ and $F_1=z^{-2}+z^{-4}$, coefficient comparison yields $S_{\ell+1,0}=S_{\ell-1,0}=1$ and, for $1\le q\le\ell$, $S_{\ell+1,q}=S_{\ell-1,q}+(2\ell+1)(2q-1)S_{\ell,q-1}$. The displayed factorial coefficients satisfy this: the ratios are $S_{\ell-1,q}/S_{\ell+1,q}=(\ell-q)(\ell-q+1)/[(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)]$ and $S_{\ell+1,q}/S_{\ell,q-1}=(2q-1)(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)/(2q)$, whose difference gives the recurrence. At the top index $q=\ell+1$, $S_{\ell+1,\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)^2S_{\ell,\ell}$; thus induction proves the stated sum at every degree. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every $S_{\ell m}$ is positive, so differentiating the finite sum gives $F_\ell'(z)<0$. For $0\le m\le\ell-1$, $S_{\ell m}/S_{\ell-1,m}=(\ell+m)/(\ell-m)\ge1$, and the degree-$\ell$ sum has one additional positive term. Hence $|h_\ell|$ decreases with $z$ and $|h_{\ell-1}|\le|h_\ell|$. For $\ell\ge1$, [F2] now implies $|h_\ell'|\le|h_{\ell-1}|+(\ell+1)|h_\ell|/z\le(1+(\ell+1)/z)|h_\ell|$; for $\ell=0$ the same bound follows by differentiating $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Differentiating the finite sum in step 1.1 cancels its $ie^{iz}$ derivative in $h_\ell'-ih_\ell$, so $|z(h_\ell'-ih_\ell)|\le\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}(m+1)A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1}$. The lowest-power term of the positive modulus sum gives $|h_\ell(z_0)|\ge A_{\ell\ell}z_0^{-\ell-1}$. For $j=\ell-m$, factorial cancellation gives $\frac{A_{\ell,\ell-j}}{A_{\ell\ell}}=\frac{2^j}{j!}\prod_{s=0}^{j-1}\frac{\ell-s}{2\ell-s}\le\frac{2^j}{j!}.$ Using $z\ge z_0$ and $m+1\le\ell+1$, the quotient in the claim is at most $(\ell+1)\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}(2z_0)^j/j!\le(\ell+1)e^{2z_0}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For integers $\ell\ge0$ and real $z>0$, write $h_\ell=h_\ell^{(1)}$ using [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]]. Then
$$|h_\ell(z)|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}S_{\ell m}z^{-2m-2},\qquad S_{\ell m}=\frac{(2m)!(\ell+m)!}{4^m(m!)^2(\ell-m)!}.$$
Consequently $|h_\ell(z)|$ is nonincreasing in $z$, $|h_{\ell-1}(z)|\le|h_\ell(z)|$ for $\ell\ge1$, and $|h_\ell'(z)|\le(1+(\ell+1)/z)|h_\ell(z)|$. For every fixed $z_0>0$ and all $z\ge z_0$,
$$\frac{|z(h_\ell'(z)-ih_\ell(z))|}{|h_\ell(z_0)|}\le(\ell+1)e^{2z_0}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-derivative outgoing Hankel convention and its radial recurrences.

[F1] [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]]: $h_\ell=(-z)^\ell(z^{-1}d/dz)^\ell(-ie^{iz}/z)$.

[F2] [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]]: $h_{\ell+1}=\ell h_\ell/z-h_\ell'$ and $h_\ell'=h_{\ell-1}-(\ell+1)h_\ell/z$ for $\ell\ge1$.

[F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $F_\ell=|h_\ell|^2$. The radial recurrence gives $h_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)h_\ell/z-h_{\ell-1}$. Also $F_\ell'=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar h_\ell h_{\ell-1})-2(\ell+1)F_\ell/z$ by [F2]. Expanding the squared modulus and eliminating the real cross term yields $F_{\ell+1}=F_{\ell-1}-(2\ell+1)F_\ell'/z-(2\ell+1)F_\ell/z^2.$ From $F_0=z^{-2}$ and $F_1=z^{-2}+z^{-4}$, coefficient comparison yields $S_{\ell+1,0}=S_{\ell-1,0}=1$ and, for $1\le q\le\ell$, $S_{\ell+1,q}=S_{\ell-1,q}+(2\ell+1)(2q-1)S_{\ell,q-1}$. ## Statement

Let $Q=Y=(0,1)^d$, let $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$ (monotonicity may be dropped; only $\epsilon_n\to0$ is used), and suppose $(u_n)$ is bounded in $L^2(Q)$. Then some subsequence two-scale converges in the sense of [[def-periodic-two-scale-convergence]] to a function $u\in L^2(Q\times Y)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A bounded real $L^2(Q)$ sequence, positive scales tending to zero, periodic rescaling, density of smooth product tests, Countable Choice, real Bolzano--Weierstrass, and Hilbert Riesz representation.

[F1] [[def-periodic-two-scale-convergence]]: convergence is tested against finite sums of compactly supported smooth slow factors and smooth periodic fast factors.

[F2] [[lem-periodic-averaging-on-cube]]: for every fixed smooth product test $\Phi$, $\|\Phi(\cdot,\cdot/\epsilon_n)\|_{L^2(Q)}\to\|\Phi\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}$; this follows by applying periodic averaging to $|\Phi(x,y)|^2$.

[F3] [[lem-product-rectangle-kernels-are-dense-in-product-l-two]], [[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]], and [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]: finite sums of smooth product tests are dense in $L^2(Q\times Y)$.

[F4] [[def-countable-choice]]: a countable dense family and the countable diagonal subsequence can be selected under Countable Choice.

[F5] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: bounded real scalar sequences have convergent subsequences.

[F6] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] and [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: every bounded real linear functional on $L^2(Q\times Y)$ is integration against a unique $L^2$ function.

[F7] [[thm-rational-box-step-functions-form-a-countable-dense-subset-of-l-p-of-rn]]: the finite-measure product space is separable, consistently with the dense test family in [F3].

## Proof




1.1 Let $M=\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$. By [F7], extend functions by zero to see that $L^2(Q\times Y)$ is separable; [F3] says the allowed test subspace is dense there. Intersect a countable base of its metric topology with that subspace and, using [F4], choose one point from every nonempty intersection. The rational span of these points is a countable dense family $D$. For each fixed $\Phi\in D$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\left|\int_Qu_n(x)\Phi(x,x/\epsilon_n)dx\right|\le M\|\Phi(\cdot,\cdot/\epsilon_n)\|_2,$ which is bounded by [F2]. Repeatedly apply [F5] to this countable family of scalar sequences and take the diagonal subsequence; on that subsequence every pairing with $D$ converges. [F7, F3, F4, F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 Denote the limit on $D$ by $L_0$. For each $\Phi\in D$, step 1.1 and [F2] give $|L_0(\Phi)|\le M\|\Phi\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}$. Limits preserve rational linearity; the bound makes $L_0$ uniformly continuous, so it has a unique continuous extension $L$ to all of the real Hilbert space $L^2(Q\times Y)$, with $\|L\|\le M$. To verify real homogeneity, first fix $\Phi\in D$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, and choose rationals $q_m\to t$. Since $q_m\Phi\in D$, $L(q_m\Phi)=q_mL_0(\Phi)$; continuity and $q_m\Phi\to t\Phi$ give $L(t\Phi)=tL(\Phi)$. For arbitrary $h\in L^2(Q\times Y)$, choose $\Phi_j\in D$ with $\Phi_j\to h$; then $t\Phi_j\to th$, and continuity gives $L(th)=tL(h)$. Additivity also passes from $D$ by continuity, so $L$ is bounded and real-linear. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 By [F6], choose $u\in L^2(Q\times Y)$ such that $L(\Phi)=\int_{Q\times Y}u\Phi$. Fix any allowed smooth product test $\Psi$ and choose $\Phi_j\in D$ with $\Phi_j\to\Psi$ in product $L^2$. Along the extracted subsequence, [F2] applied to $\Psi-\Phi_j$ gives $\limsup_n\left|\int_Qu_n(\Psi-\Phi_j)(x,x/\epsilon_n)dx\right|\le M\|\Psi-\Phi_j\|_2.$ Also $|L(\Psi-\Phi_j)|\le M\|\Psi-\Phi_j\|_2$. Since the pairings for $\Phi_j$ converge to $L(\Phi_j)$, letting $j\to\infty$ proves convergence for $\Psi$ to $L(\Psi)=\int u\Psi$. This is precisely the two-scale convergence in [F1]. [F6, F2, F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For the front in [[ex-phase-field-allen-cahn-stationary-front]], the interval where $|u_\varepsilon(x)|\le\frac12$ has width
$$W_\varepsilon=2\sqrt{2\kappa}\,\varepsilon\,\operatorname{artanh}(1/2).$$
If a uniform sample grid has spacing $h>W_\varepsilon$ and the front is centered halfway between two sample points, no grid point lies in that transition interval. This gives a precise unresolved-interface configuration; it is not a sufficient resolution criterion.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exact front profile and positive parameters $\kappa,\varepsilon$.

[F1] [[ex-phase-field-allen-cahn-stationary-front]]: $u_\varepsilon(x)=\tanh(x/(\sqrt{2\kappa}\,\varepsilon))$ and its transition is centered at $x=0$.

## Verification

1.1 Since $\tanh$ is strictly increasing and $\tanh(\operatorname{artanh}(1/2))=1/2$, the endpoints of $|u_\varepsilon|\le1/2$ are $x=\pm\sqrt{2\kappa}\,\varepsilon\operatorname{artanh}(1/2)$. Subtracting them gives $W_\varepsilon$ as stated. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Place sample points at $(j+\frac12)h$ for $j\in\mathbb Z$. Their distance from the front center is at least $h/2>W_\varepsilon/2$, so every sample point lies outside the transition interval from step 1.1. The grid therefore records no sample with $|u_\varepsilon|\le1/2$. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the interpolant $I_h$ of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], every cell weight is nonnegative and the weights sum to one by
[[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]. Hence
$V\le W$ on grid nodes implies $I_hV\le I_hW$, and
$\|I_hV\|_{\infty}\le\|V\|_{\infty}$. If $\phi\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ and $V_i=\phi(x_i)$, then
$$\|I_hV-\phi\|_{\infty}\le\frac18\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2\|\partial_{jj}\phi\|_{\infty}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The periodic grid and tensor interpolant, nodal arrays $V,W$, and a periodic $C^2$ function $\phi$.

[F1] The local grid is the unit-period specialization of the periodic tensor grid, with $N_j\ge3$, and its interpolant has nonnegative tensor weights summing to one, hence is order-preserving and $L^\infty$-contractive ([[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]], [[lem-periodic-tensor-interpolant-is-convex-and-linf-contracting]]).

[F2] If the second derivative of a $C^2$ function is bounded by $M$ on an interval, its first-order Taylor remainder from an endpoint has magnitude at most $M|x-a|^2/2$ ([[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]).

## Proof

1.1 The supplier result in [F1] says each evaluation is a convex combination of the corner data. Applying this to $W-V\ge0$ proves order preservation, and applying it to $V$ and $-V$ proves the sup-norm bound. [F1, algebra]

1.2 In one coordinate, let $x=x_i+\theta h$ with $0\le\theta\le1$ and let $L_h\phi(x)=(1-\theta)\phi(x_i)+\theta\phi(x_i+h)$. Taylor-expand both endpoints about $x$. By [F2], the linear terms cancel after weighting and $$|L_h\phi(x)-\phi(x)|\le\frac{h^2}{2}\|\phi''\|_{\infty}\bigl((1-\theta)\theta^2+\theta(1-\theta)^2\bigr)=\frac{h^2}{2}\theta(1-\theta)\|\phi''\|_{\infty}\le\frac{h^2}{8}\|\phi''\|_{\infty}.$$ This calculation also holds on the periodic seam by taking a periodic lift of the cell. [F2, algebra]

2.1 Write the tensor interpolant as the product of the one-coordinate interpolation operators $I_j$. Each $I_j$ has sup-norm at most one by step 1.1. The identity $$I_1\cdots I_d-I=\sum_{j=1}^d I_1\cdots I_{j-1}(I_j-I)$$ and the one-dimensional bound of step 1.2 give the claimed sum of errors. This proves the statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, $a>0$, $s=\nu+d/2$, and the normalized Matérn kernel with spectral density $w(\xi)=A(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-s}$ from [[def-normalized-matern-spectral-kernel]]. For a list of $N\ge2$ distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\subset\mathbb R^d$, put $q=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$. There is $c=c(d,\nu,a)>0$ such that if $0<q\le1$, then
$$\lambda_{\min}(K_X)\ge c q^{2\nu},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N,\qquad \kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2\nu}.$$
The eigenvalues and condition number are those of the exact real symmetric positive-definite matrix. For $N=1$, $K_X=[1]$ and $\kappa_2(K_X)=1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Fixed Matérn parameters, $N\ge2$ distinct sites, and $0<q\le1$.

[F1] The spectral density is positive, $w(\xi)=A(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-s}$, and $k(z)=\int w(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}d\xi$. ([[def-normalized-matern-spectral-kernel]], [[lem-matern-spectral-integral-and-normalization]])

[F2] The Matérn kernel is real and even, with $k(0)=1$, so its Gram matrix is real symmetric and every diagonal entry is one. ([[lem-matern-spectral-integral-and-normalization]])

[F3] Linear changes of variables scale Lebesgue measure by the absolute determinant; balls are measurable with positive finite measure, translations preserve measure, and Lebesgue measure is finitely additive on disjoint measurable sets. ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]])

[F4] For a real symmetric matrix, its smallest and largest eigenvalues are the minimum and maximum Rayleigh quotients. ([[cor-rayleigh-quotient-extreme-eigenvalue-characterisation]], [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]])

[F5] A smooth bump can be chosen equal to one on the half-radius ball and supported in the unit ball. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]])

[F6] The induced matrix 2-norm of a symmetric matrix is its largest absolute eigenvalue. ([[lem-symmetric-matrix-operator-norm-rayleigh]], [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]])

[F7] The nonnegative integral is monotone and the modulus of an integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus. ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]])

[F8] Smooth compactly supported functions are Schwartz, and the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform maps Schwartz functions to Schwartz functions. ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]])

[F9] Euler's formula gives $|e^{it}|=1$ for real $t$ and $\overline{e^{it}}=e^{-it}$. ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]])

[F10] For $s>0$, $r\mapsto r^s$ is increasing on $(0,\infty)$ by its positive derivative and the mean value theorem, so $0<x\le y$ implies $x^{-s}\ge y^{-s}$; positive-base power laws also give $(r^{-2})^{-s}=r^{2s}$. ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[thm-real-power-laws]])

[F11] The positive p-series $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-p}$ converges for $p>1$. ([[thm-p-series-real-exponents]])

[A1] Countable Choice is the measure-theoretic hypothesis inherited from the ball, Lebesgue and polar-measure suppliers; no choice of sites or window functions is made from an arbitrary family. ([[def-countable-choice]])



**Proof technique:** localized spectral window, packing, and Rayleigh quotients.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** localized spectral window, packing, and Rayleigh quotients.

**Given:** The hypotheses above.

1.1 By [F5] choose a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^d\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $\overline B(0,1/2)$ and supported in $B(0,1)$. Set $\eta(\xi)=(\rho(\xi)+\rho(-\xi))/2$. Then $\eta$ is smooth, even, nonnegative, at most one, still equals one on the half-radius ball, and is supported in the unit ball. Define $\psi(z)=\int\eta(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}d\xi$. Reflection invariance of Lebesgue measure [F3] and Euler's formula [F9] make $\psi$ real and even, and monotonicity [F7] gives $\psi(0)=\int\eta\ge\lambda(B(0,1/2))>0$. [F3, F5, F7, F9, A1, algebra, choose]

2.1 Since $\eta$ is smooth and compactly supported, it is Schwartz by [F8], so $\widehat\eta$ is Schwartz and $\psi(z)=\widehat\eta(-z)$ is Schwartz as well. For $|z|\ge1$, choose a coordinate $j$ with $|z_j|\ge|z|/\sqrt d$; the Schwartz seminorm $\sup_\xi|\xi_j^M\widehat\eta(\xi)|<\infty$ gives $|\psi(z)|\le C_M|z|^{-M}$. For $|z|\le1$, [F7] and $|e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}|=1$ from [F9] give $|\psi(z)|\le\int\eta$. Combining the two bounds yields $|\psi(z)|\le C'_M(1+|z|)^{-M}$. [F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $i$. The open balls $B(x_j,q)$ are pairwise disjoint because center distances are at least $2q$. If $n\le|x_i-x_j|/q<n+1$, then $B(x_j,q)\subset B(x_i,(n+2)q)$. Translation invariance and dilation change of variables in [F3] give $\lambda(B(x,r))=r^d\lambda(B(0,1))$; this unit-ball measure is finite and positive. Finite additivity on the disjoint balls therefore bounds the number of such $j$ by $(n+2)^d$. Hence, for any integer $M>d+1$ and $T\ge1$, [step 2.1] yields the uniform row-sum estimate $$\sum_{j\ne i}\left|\psi\!\left(T(x_i-x_j)/q\right)\right|\le C_MT^{-M}\sum_{n\ge1}(n+2)^dn^{-M}.$$ For $n\ge1$, $(n+2)^d\le3^dn^d$, so this series is bounded by $3^d\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-(M-d)}$, which converges by [F11] because $M-d>1$. Choose one fixed $T$ large enough that this upper bound is at most $\psi(0)/2$. [F3, F11, A1, step 2.1, given, choose]

4.1 For any $c\in\mathbb C^N$, the quadratic form of $H_{ij}=\psi(T(x_i-x_j)/q)$ satisfies $$c^*Hc\ge\left(\psi(0)-\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}|H_{ij}|\right)\|c\|_2^2\ge\frac{\psi(0)}2\|c\|_2^2,$$ because each off-diagonal pair is bounded using $2|c_i||c_j|\le|c_i|^2+|c_j|^2$. By the change of variables $\zeta=(q/T)\xi$, $$\int_{|\xi|\le T/q}\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi\ge\int\eta(q\xi/T)\left|\sum_jc_je^{-2\pi ix_j\cdot\xi}\right|^2d\xi=(T/q)^d c^*Hc.$$ The first inequality uses $0\le\eta\le1$ and support in the unit ball. [F3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 On $|\xi|\le T/q$ and $q\le1$, set $B=(a^2+4\pi^2T^2)q^{-2}$. Then $a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2\le a^2+4\pi^2T^2/q^2\le B$. Monotonicity and the power laws [F10] give $$w(\xi)\ge A B^{-s}=A\left(a^2+4\pi^2T^2\right)^{-s}q^{2s}.$$ Using the Fourier quadratic-form identity from [F1] and step 4.1 gives $c^*K_Xc\ge c_0q^{2s-d}\|c\|_2^2=c_0q^{2\nu}\|c\|_2^2$ for a constant $c_0>0$ independent of $X,q,N$. Thus [F4] yields $\lambda_{\min}(K_X)\ge c_0q^{2\nu}$. [F1, F4, F10, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 By [F4], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis and write $K_X=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. If $Q=(q_{ij})$, then $$\operatorname{tr}(K_X)=\sum_i(K_X)_{ii}=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j=N,$$ since each column of $Q$ has unit norm and [F2] gives diagonal entries $k(0)=1$. By step 5.1 all eigenvalues are positive, so $\lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N$. In this eigenbasis the induced 2-norms of $K_X$ and $K_X^{-1}$ are $\lambda_{\max}$ and $1/\lambda_{\min}$, respectively, by [F6]. The definition $\kappa_2(K_X)=\|K_X\|_2\|K_X^{-1}\|_2$ therefore gives $\kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2\nu}$. The $N=1$ case follows directly from $k(0)=1$ and the same definition. [F2, F4, F6, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

$$\lambda_{\min}(K_X)\ge c q^{2\nu},\qquad \lambda_{\max}(K_X)\le N,\qquad \kappa_2(K_X)\le c^{-1}Nq^{-2\nu}.$$
The eigenvalues and condition number are those of the exact real symmetric positive-definite matrix. For $N=1$, $K_X=[1]$ and $\kappa_2(K_X)=1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Fixed Matérn parameters, $N\ge2$ distinct sites, and $0<q\le1$.

[F1] The spectral density is positive, $w(\xi)=A(a^2+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-s}$, and $k(z)=\int w(\xi)e^{2\pi iz\cdot\xi}d\xi$. ([[def-normalized-matern-spectral-kernel]], [[lem-matern-spectral-integral-and-normalization]])

[F2] The Matérn kernel is real and even, with $k(0)=1$, so its Gram matrix is real symmetric and every diagonal entry is one. ([[lem-matern-spectral-integral-and-normalization]])

[F3] Linear changes of variables scale Lebesgue measure by the absolute determinant; balls are measurable with positive finite measure, translations preserve measure, and Lebesgue measure is finitely additive on disjoint measurable sets. ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]])

[F4] For a real symmetric matrix, its smallest and largest eigenvalues are the minimum and maximum Rayleigh quotients. ([[cor-rayleigh-quotient-extreme-eigenvalue-characterisation]], [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]])

[F5] A smooth bump can be chosen equal to one on the half-radius ball and supported in the unit ball. ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]])

[F6] The induced matrix 2-norm of a symmetric matrix is its largest absolute eigenvalue. ([[lem-symmetric-matrix-operator-norm-rayleigh]], [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]])

[F7] The nonnegative integral is monotone and the modulus of an integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus. ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]])

[F8] Smooth compactly supported functions are Schwartz, and the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform maps Schwartz functions to Schwartz functions. ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], [[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]])

[F9] Euler's formula gives $|e^{it}|=1$ for real $t$ and $\overline{e^{it}}=e^{-it}$. ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]])

[F10] For $s>0$, $r\mapsto r^s$ is increasing on $(0,\infty)$ by its positive derivative and the mean value theorem, so $0<x\le y$ implies $x^{-s}\ge y^{-s}$; positive-base power laws also give $(r^{-2})^{-s}=r^{2s}$. [F11] The positive p-series $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-p}$ converges for $p>1$. ([[thm-p-series-real-exponents]])

[A1] Countable Choice is the measure-theoretic hypothesis inherited from the ball, Lebesgue and polar-measure suppliers; no choice of sites or window functions is made from an arbitrary family. ([[def-countable-choice]])
