## Statement

In the multilevel transform of [[def-na-d4-periodic-multilevel-transform]], a detail row at stage $\ell$ has $2^{J-\ell}$ translates, is supported on at most $3(2^\ell-1)+1$ consecutive input indices on a periodic lift, has Euclidean norm $1$, and annihilates every affine function of the lifted sample index. Its $\ell^1$ norm, meaning the sum of absolute row entries, is at most the square root of its support size. Since $1\le\ell\le J-2$, this support has fewer than $N=2^J$ indices and so its lifted support contains no repeated residue modulo $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $J\ge3$, $N=2^J$, the D4 filter pair, and the multilevel periodic procedure defined above.

[F1] [[def-na-d4-periodic-multilevel-transform]]: stage $\ell$ applies the four-tap low-pass filter to the approximation branch $\ell-1$ times before taking a four-tap high-pass detail, with all indices periodic modulo the current length.

[F2] [[thm-na-daubechies-d4-filter-qmf-and-two-moments]]: $\sum g_r=0$ and $\sum r g_r=0$, and the D4 filters satisfy the QMF conditions.

[F3] [[thm-na-periodic-orthogonal-compact-filter-dwt-inverse-parseval]]: every applied one-level D4 analysis matrix and their multilevel composition are orthogonal.

## Proof

1.1 Expanding the recursion shows that the detail row at stage $\ell$, translated to its first input index, has taps at indices $t=2^{\ell-1}r+2^{\ell-2}s_{\ell-1}+\cdots+2s_2+s_1$, where each of $r,s_1,\ldots,s_{\ell-1}$ ranges over $\{0,1,2,3\}$; its coefficient is $g_r\prod_{v=1}^{\ell-1}h_{s_v}$. This follows by substituting the low-pass sum at each earlier stage into the current high-pass sum. The largest such index is $3(2^\ell-1)$, so the row is supported in at most $3(2^\ell-1)+1$ consecutive locations. Because $\ell\le J-2$, this number is $3\cdot2^\ell-2\le3\cdot2^{J-2}-2<N$, so the locations are distinct modulo $N$. [given, F1, construct, induction, algebra]

2.1 Regard the effective taps in step 1.1 before reducing their input positions modulo $N$. A low-pass stage maps an affine input sequence $p(n)=\alpha+\beta n$ to an affine sequence: $\sum_{s=0}^3h_sp(2k+s)=2\beta k\sum h_s+\alpha\sum h_s+\beta\sum s h_s$, which is affine in $k$. Repeating this argument keeps the coarse sequence affine. The next high-pass stage applied to an affine sequence $A+Bk$ gives $A\sum g_s+B(2k\sum g_s+\sum s g_s)=0$ by [F2]. Therefore the effective detail tap row has zero sum and zero first moment. Periodic reduction only assigns these taps to residues; because step 1.1 gives fewer than $N$ taps, each residue is unique and the row can be lifted back to the same support interval. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], each row of the full multilevel analysis matrix has squared Euclidean norm $1$. If its support has $S$ locations with coefficients $z_1,\ldots,z_S$, then $(\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|)^2\le S\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|^2=S$, since $S\sum_i|z_i|^2-(\sum_i|z_i|)^2=\sum_{i<j}(|z_i|-|z_j|)^2\ge0$. Hence its $\ell^1$ norm is at most $\sqrt S$. The detail block at stage $\ell$ has the length of the current approximation after downsampling, namely $N/2^\ell=2^{J-\ell}$ rows. This and the affine cancellation from step 2.1 establish every clause of the Statement. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

In the multilevel transform of [[def-na-d4-periodic-multilevel-transform]], a detail row at stage $\ell$ has $2^{J-\ell}$ translates, is supported on at most $3(2^\ell-1)+1$ consecutive input indices on a periodic lift, has Euclidean norm $1$, and annihilates every affine function of the lifted sample index. Its $\ell^1$ norm, meaning the sum of absolute row entries, is at most the square root of its support size. Since $1\le\ell\le J-2$, this support has fewer than $N=2^J$ indices and so its lifted support contains no repeated residue modulo $N$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $J\ge3$, $N=2^J$, the D4 filter pair, and the multilevel periodic procedure defined above.

[F1] [[def-na-d4-periodic-multilevel-transform]]: stage $\ell$ applies the four-tap low-pass filter to the approximation branch $\ell-1$ times before taking a four-tap high-pass detail, with all indices periodic modulo the current length.

[F2] [[thm-na-daubechies-d4-filter-qmf-and-two-moments]]: $\sum g_r=0$ and $\sum r g_r=0$, and the D4 filters satisfy the QMF conditions.

[F3] [[thm-na-periodic-orthogonal-compact-filter-dwt-inverse-parseval]]: every applied one-level D4 analysis matrix and their multilevel composition are orthogonal.

## Proof

1.1 Expanding the recursion shows that the detail row at stage $\ell$, translated to its first input index, has taps at indices $t=2^{\ell-1}r+2^{\ell-2}s_{\ell-1}+\cdots+2s_2+s_1$, where each of $r,s_1,\ldots,s_{\ell-1}$ ranges over $\{0,1,2,3\}$; its coefficient is $g_r\prod_{v=1}^{\ell-1}h_{s_v}$. This follows by substituting the low-pass sum at each earlier stage into the current high-pass sum. The largest such index is $3(2^\ell-1)$, so the row is supported in at most $3(2^\ell-1)+1$ consecutive locations. Because $\ell\le J-2$, this number is $3\cdot2^\ell-2\le3\cdot2^{J-2}-2<N$, so the locations are distinct modulo $N$. [given, F1, construct, induction, algebra]

2.1 Regard the effective taps in step 1.1 before reducing their input positions modulo $N$. A low-pass stage maps an affine input sequence $p(n)=\alpha+\beta n$ to an affine sequence: $\sum_{s=0}^3h_sp(2k+s)=2\beta k\sum h_s+\alpha\sum h_s+\beta\sum s h_s$, which is affine in $k$. Repeating this argument keeps the coarse sequence affine. The next high-pass stage applied to an affine sequence $A+Bk$ gives $A\sum g_s+B(2k\sum g_s+\sum s g_s)=0$ by [F2]. Therefore the effective detail tap row has zero sum and zero first moment. Periodic reduction only assigns these taps to residues; because step 1.1 gives fewer than $N$ taps, each residue is unique and the row can be lifted back to the same support interval. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], each row of the full multilevel analysis matrix has squared Euclidean norm $1$. If its support has $S$ locations with coefficients $z_1,\ldots,z_S$, then $(\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|)^2\le S\sum_{i=1}^S|z_i|^2=S$, since $S\sum_i|z_i|^2-(\sum_i|z_i|)^2=\sum_{i<j}(|z_i|-|z_j|)^2\ge0$. Hence its $\ell^1$ norm is at most $\sqrt S$. The detail block at stage $\ell$ has the length of the current approximation after downsampling, namely $N/2^\ell=2^{J-\ell}$ rows. This and the affine cancellation from step 2.1 establish every clause of the Statement. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ be points in $\mathbb D^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, with
$O_d\ne0$ under the determinant convention in
[[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]]. By
[[lem-nondegenerate-dyadic-simplex-determines-unique-sphere]], there is a unique
sphere $S(c,r)=\{x:\sum_j(x_j-c_j)^2=r^2\}$ through $p_0,\ldots,p_d$. For
$q=p_{d+1}$ and its lifted determinant $L_d$,
$$
L_d=-O_d\left(\sum_j(q_j-c_j)^2-r^2\right).
$$
Consequently $O_dL_d$ is positive for $q$ inside the sphere, zero on it, and
negative outside it.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The point and lifted determinant row conventions in [[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]], $O_d\ne0$, and a sphere $S(c,r)$ through $p_0,\ldots,p_d$.

[F1] [[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]]: $O_d$ is the determinant of rows $(p_i,1)$ and $L_d$ is the determinant of rows $(p_i,\sum_jp_{i,j}^2,1)$.

[F2] [[def-complete-ordered-real-field]]: the coordinates, sphere center, and radius are in an ordered real field, so positive squares and their order comparisons have their usual meanings.

[F3] [[lem-nondegenerate-dyadic-simplex-determines-unique-sphere]]: every base tuple with $O_d\ne0$ determines a unique center $c$ and nonnegative radius $r$ whose sphere contains all base points.

[A1] The sphere equation is $\sum_j(p_{i,j}-c_j)^2=r^2$ for $i=0,\ldots,d$, and $q=p_{d+1}$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $A$ be the $d\times d$ matrix with rows $p_i-p_0$ for $i=1,\ldots,d$. Subtracting row $p_0$ from the other rows of the matrix defining $O_d$ leaves its determinant unchanged: the Leibniz formula is linear in each row, and the added determinant has two equal rows, whose terms cancel in pairs under the transposition of those rows. Expansion along the final column then gives $\det A=(-1)^dO_d$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Expanding the equal sphere radii in [A1], which exist uniquely by [F3], gives $\sum_jp_{i,j}^2-\sum_jp_{0,j}^2=2\sum_jc_j(p_{i,j}-p_{0,j})$ for $i=1,\ldots,d$. For $q$, put $R=\sum_j(q_j-c_j)^2-r^2$; the same expansion gives $\sum_jq_j^2-\sum_jp_{0,j}^2=2\sum_jc_j(q_j-p_{0,j})+R$. [given, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

2.1 Subtract row $p_0$ from the other rows of the matrix defining $L_d$, then expand along its final column. The cofactor sign is $(-1)^{d+3}$, and the remaining determinant has rows $(p_i-p_0,\sum_jp_{i,j}^2-\sum_jp_{0,j}^2)$, including the row for $q$. Subtracting $2c_j$ times coordinate column $j$ from the last column makes its first $d$ entries zero by [step 1.2] and its final entry $R$. The resulting determinant is $\det A\,R$. These row and column operations preserve the Leibniz determinant: multilinearity in columns follows from the same permutation formula, and the added determinant has equal columns whose terms cancel in pairs under their transposition. Thus $L_d=(-1)^{d+3}\det A\,R=-O_dR$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Multiplication by $O_d$ gives $O_dL_d=-O_d^2R$. Since $O_d\ne0$, $O_d^2>0$ in the ordered field [F2]; therefore the product is positive exactly when $R<0$, zero exactly when $R=0$, and negative exactly when $R>0$. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Whenever [[alg-floating-filter-for-geometric-determinants]] returns
`positive` or `negative`, the exact determinant has that same sign. An
`inconclusive` or nonfinite result carries no sign claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite matrix $M$ and a completed filter evaluation satisfying the stated model and range hypotheses in [[alg-floating-filter-for-geometric-determinants]].

[F1] [[alg-floating-filter-for-geometric-determinants]]: the filter returns a sign only if its exact dyadic interval $[\widehat D-E,\widehat D+E]$ excludes zero.

[F2] [[lem-leibniz-determinant-forward-error-bound]]: under the filter's operation hypotheses, $|\widehat D-\det M|\le\gamma_q S$.

[F3] [[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]: every exact node value of a finite expression DAG with finite operation results belongs to its computed interval enclosure.

[F4] [[lem-directed-dyadic-rounding-enclosure-and-error]]: directed upward rounding encloses each finite exact endpoint from above.

## Proof

1.1 The filter's absolute-term DAG evaluates $S$ from [F2]. Its returned upper endpoint $U$ satisfies $S\le U$ by [F3]. The definition of $E$ and [F4] give $E\ge\gamma_qU$, hence $E\ge\gamma_qS$. [given, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Combining [F2] with [step 1.1] yields $|\widehat D-\det M|\le E$, so $\det M\in[\widehat D-E,\widehat D+E]$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 If the algorithm returns positive, [F1] says $\widehat D-E>0$; by [step 2.1], $\det M\ge\widehat D-E>0$. If it returns negative, then $\widehat D+E<0$ and [step 2.1] gives $\det M\le\widehat D+E<0$. In all other cases it returns no sign. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

During budgeted CP-ALS, each successful exact block update does not increase the squared Frobenius residual. A rank-deficient-design halt leaves the factor matrices unchanged, so it leaves the objective unchanged. Consequently, the objective is nonincreasing over every sequence of completed exact block updates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The tensor, initial factor matrices, finite budget, and exact-arithmetic procedure of budgeted CP-ALS.

[F1] [[alg-budgeted-cp-alternating-least-squares]]: each successful block replaces one factor by the exact least-squares minimizer with other factors fixed; a rank-deficient design halts without changing the current factor.

[F2] [[lem-full-column-rank-matrix-least-squares-solution]]: a full-column-rank design has a unique Frobenius least-squares minimizer, and its residual is no larger than that of any other candidate factor.

## Proof

1.1 Fix a successful mode-$k$ update and keep all other factor matrices fixed. The residual objective as a function of the replaced factor $X$ is $\|A_{(k)}-XZ_k^{\mathsf T}\|_F^2$. Taking adjoints preserves the Frobenius norm and rewrites it as $\|A_{(k)}^*-\overline{Z_k}X^*\|_F^2$. Since $Z_k$ has full column rank, so does $\overline{Z_k}$; [F2] therefore makes the algorithm's update the unique minimizer of this block objective. The old factor is an admissible candidate, so the updated objective is at most the old one. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A rank-deficient-design branch stops before changing a factor, so the objective is identical before and after that branch. Every other executed update satisfies step 1.1; chaining these finitely many inequalities across any completed part of a sweep proves the objective is nonincreasing through all successful exact block updates. This asserts no convergence or global optimality. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(4,1,0,0)\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}$, take target
rank $k=2$, oversampling $p=2$, and draw $\Omega\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}$
with iid standard real Gaussian entries. The randomized range finder returns
$QQ^*A=A$ almost surely, so its spectral error is zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice for the finite Gaussian law, and the fixed diagonal matrix and the Gaussian range-finder draw.

[F1] The algorithm returns an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$ and then $QQ^*A$ ([[alg-gaussian-randomized-range-finder]]).

[F2] Orthogonal SVD coordinates preserve the iid Gaussian law ([[lem-gaussian-matrix-orthogonal-unitary-invariance-and-block-independence]]).

[F3] A wide Gaussian matrix has full row rank almost surely ([[lem-wide-gaussian-matrix-has-full-row-rank-almost-surely]]).

## Verification

1.1 The displayed diagonal matrix has rank $2$ and SVD $A=U\Sigma V^*$ with $U=V=I$ and $\Sigma_2=0$. Write $\Omega_1$ for its first two rows. By [F2]–[F3], $\Omega_1$ has row rank $2$ almost surely. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For every such draw, $A\Omega=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\\0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\Omega_1$ has range exactly $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$, since the first two rows of $\Omega$ have rank $2$ and multiplication by $\operatorname{diag}(4,1)$ preserves rank. Thus $QQ^*$ is the projector onto this span and $QQ^*A=A$. [step 1.1, F1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a finite triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites of affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $E$ the number of edges, and $T$ the number of bounded triangular faces. Then
$$3T=2E-k,\qquad n-E+T=1,$$
and consequently $T=2n-2-k$ and $E=3n-3-k$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites, with its connected 1-skeleton.

[F1] [[def-planar-delaunay-voronoi-structures]]: a triangulation covers the convex hull with nondegenerate triangles meeting in common faces; its connected 1-skeleton has precisely those bounded triangular faces and one unbounded exterior face.

[F2] [[def-planar-delaunay-voronoi-structures]]: the triangles partition the convex hull, meet along common complete faces, and the hull boundary is subdivided at every boundary site.

## Proof

1.1 Let $h$ be the number of hull corners, meaning the boundary sites that are not in the relative interior of any hull edge. Their interior angles sum to $(h-2)\pi$, because a convex $h$-gon is divided into $h-2$ triangles by diagonals from one corner. Each of the other $k-h$ boundary sites has straight angle $\pi$. Around each interior site the incident triangle angles sum to $2\pi$, while at each boundary site they sum to its hull angle. Counting all triangle angles gives $\pi T=2\pi(n-k)+(h-2)\pi+(k-h)\pi=(2n-k-2)\pi$, hence $T=2n-2-k$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Count incidences between triangle sides and edges. Each triangle contributes three. An interior edge has one triangle on each of its two local sides; a hull edge has exactly one incident triangle inside the convex hull. Since the hull boundary has $k$ sites, it has $k$ subdivided boundary edges. Thus $3T=2(E-k)+k=2E-k$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Substituting the value of $T$ from step 1.1 into step 1.2 gives $E=3n-3-k$. Consequently $n-E+T=n-(3n-3-k)+(2n-2-k)=1$, proving both identities. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $A=(1,1,1)^T$, $b=e_1$, and let $S\in\mathbb R^{2\times3}$
have rows $q_1^T=(1,1,1)/\sqrt3$ and
$q_2^T=(2,-1,-1)/\sqrt6$. Compute the original and sketched least-squares
minimizers and residuals.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The matrices above and an exact-arithmetic sketch-and-solve execution that converges.

[F1] The sketch is an $\varepsilon$-embedding for a subspace when it preserves every squared norm there within factors $1\pm\varepsilon$ ([[def-oblivious-l2-subspace-embedding]]).

[F2] A converged exact sketch-and-solve execution returns a minimizer of the sketched least-squares objective ([[thm-sketch-and-solve-exact-minimizer]]).

[F3] If the embedding subspace includes $\operatorname{Ran}(A)$ and $b$, the exact residual bound follows from [[thm-sketch-and-solve-residual-guarantee]].

## Verification

1.1 Direct calculation gives $\|q_1\|_2=\|q_2\|_2=1$ and $q_1^Tq_2=0$. Also $A=\sqrt3q_1$ and $b=(1/\sqrt3)q_1+\sqrt{2/3}\,q_2$, so $\operatorname{span}(A,b)=\operatorname{span}(q_1,q_2)$. The rows of $S$ form an orthonormal basis of this subspace; hence $S$ preserves its squared norms exactly and [F1] holds for every $0<\varepsilon<1$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 For real $x$, $\|Ax-b\|_2^2=(x-1)^2+x^2+x^2=3(x-1/3)^2+2/3$. Thus the original minimizer is $x_*=1/3$ and its residual squared is $2/3$. [algebra]

1.3 The sketch gives $SA=(\sqrt3,0)^T$ and $Sb=(1/\sqrt3,\sqrt{2/3})^T$. Therefore $\|SAx-Sb\|_2^2=3(x-1/3)^2+2/3$; by [F2], $\widehat x=1/3$, with sketched residual squared $2/3$. Substitution into $A\widehat x-b=(-2/3,1/3,1/3)^T$ gives physical residual squared $2/3$ as well. [F2, algebra]

2.1 The fixed-subspace embedding hypothesis in [F3] is satisfied by step 1.1, and the computed minimizer in step 1.3 satisfies $\|A\widehat x-b\|_2^2=2/3\le((1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon))(2/3)$ for $0<\varepsilon<1$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X\succeq0$ be the stabilizing DARE solution, $G=BR^{-1}B^*$, and
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad A_c=A-B(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Then
$$N\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=M\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}A_c.$$
The pencil $(N,M)$ is regular. Its homogeneous determinant has n roots strictly inside the unit disk and n roots strictly outside the closed unit disk, with infinite roots counted in the latter group. Thus it has no unit-circle roots, even if $A$ is singular, and $\operatorname{Ran}\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}$ is its stable deflating graph.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The DARE data and stabilizing solution from [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]].

[F1] [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]]: $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S=R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c=A-BS^{-1}B^*XA$ is Schur stable.

[F2] [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]]: $G=BR^{-1}B^*$ and the DARE residual is $Q+A^*XA-A^*XB S^{-1}B^*XA-X$.

[F3] [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]: each finite-dimensional non-negative self-adjoint matrix has a non-negative square root.

[F4] [[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]]: a square pencil is regular when its homogeneous determinant is not the zero polynomial.

[F5] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: determinants multiply under finite square matrix products, so the determinant is unchanged by the determinant-one shears used below.

[F6] [[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]: the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries; in particular, the two unit-triangular shears below have determinant one.

[F7] [[lem-block-upper-triangular-pencil-determinant-factorizes]]: the homogeneous determinant of a block upper-triangular pencil factors across its diagonal blocks.

[F8] [[thm-spectrum-is-the-root-set-of-the-characteristic-polynomial]]: finite eigenvalues of a matrix are exactly the roots of its characteristic polynomial.

[F9] [[cor-every-complex-polynomial-splits-into-linear-factors]]: each complex characteristic polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ roots counted with algebraic multiplicity.

[F10] [[cor-endomorphisms-over-an-algebraically-closed-field-have-jordan-form]]: generalized eigenvectors span a complex finite-dimensional space, with total dimension counted by algebraic multiplicity.

## Proof

1.1 The matrix $I+GX$ is invertible. Indeed, if $(I+GX)v=0$, multiplication by $v^*X$ gives $v^*Xv+(Xv)^*G(Xv)=0.$ Both summands are nonnegative. By [F3], $v^*Xv=0$ implies $Xv=0$, and the original equation then gives $v=0$. Also $S=R+B^*XB\succ0$ by [F1]. The identity $(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS^{-1}B^*X$ is verified by multiplying the right side by $I+GX$: the extra term is $B[R^{-1}-S^{-1}-S^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}]B^*X=0$, since $S=R+B^*XB$. Therefore $A_c=(I+GX)^{-1}A$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The DARE and the identity in step 1.1 imply $X-Q=A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A=A^*XA_c$. Consequently, $N\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A\\X-Q\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}I+GX\\A^*X\end{bmatrix}A_c =M\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}A_c.$ This proves the deflating graph identity. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $T_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\X&I\end{bmatrix}$ and $L_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}$. By [F6] both are block triangular with identity diagonal and determinant one. For arbitrary homogeneous coordinates $[\alpha:\beta]$, $L_X(\beta N-\alpha M)T_X= \begin{bmatrix} (I+GX)(\beta A_c-\alpha I)&-\alpha G\\ 0&\beta I-\alpha A_c^* \end{bmatrix}.$ The lower-left block vanishes by $X-Q=A^*XA_c$; the lower-right block uses $(I+GX)^{-1}G=G(I+XG)^{-1}$ and $I-X(I+GX)^{-1}G=(I+XG)^{-1}$. Taking determinants and using [F5] and [F7] gives $\det(\beta N-\alpha M)=\det(I+GX)\det(\beta A_c-\alpha I)\det(\beta I-\alpha A_c^*).$ The first homogeneous factor has $n$ roots, counted with multiplicity; all are finite and equal to eigenvalues of $A_c$, hence strictly inside the disk by [F1] and [F8]. The roots of $A_c^*$ are the conjugates of those of $A_c$, since $\det(\mu I-A_c^*)=\overline{\det(\overline\mu I-A_c)}$; hence each nonzero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ has modulus less than one. The second factor has $n$ roots, counted with multiplicity: each finite root is the reciprocal of a nonzero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ and therefore has modulus greater than one, while every zero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ contributes a root at $\beta=0$, which is infinite. The root counts follow from [F9], with finite eigenvalues identified by [F8]. Neither factor vanishes on $|\alpha|=|\beta|$, so the pencil is regular with the stated root split. The homogeneous determinant is invariant under these transforms because [F5] gives multiplicativity and both shear determinants equal one by [F6]. Finally, $(I+GX)$ is invertible by step 1.1, so $M[I;X]$ has full column rank. A Jordan basis of $A_c$ from [F10], together with $N[I;X]=M[I;X]A_c$ from step 2.1, shows that the graph carries all $n$ stable finite root chains; the determinant factorization shows there are exactly $n$ stable roots in total, so this is the stable deflating graph. This uses no inverse of $A$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

In the dense arithmetic model, a single-matrix Schur reduction or regular-pair QZ reduction of order $n$ with at most $s$ Francis/QZ sweeps has core work $O(n^3+sn^2)$: the initial Hessenberg or Hessenberg-triangular reduction costs $O(n^3)$ and each full bulge-chasing sweep costs $O(n^2)$. Forming a graph candidate by solving $XU_1=U_2$ with dense $n\times n$ factorization, $n$ right-hand sides, and residual multiplication costs $O(n^3)$.

After an order-$d$ reduction, finite stable-block reordering with $k$ actual attempts costs $O(d^2+kd)$ scalar operations. If the form has $b$ diagonal blocks and $I$ complementary-before-selected inversions, then $I\le b(b-1)/2$; successful ordering requires $K\ge I$ and enough scalar/evaluator budget $W$ for the entire execution, including validation, label and inversion scans, all $I$ swaps, and the final ordering scan. For a Riccati pencil or Hamiltonian with $d=2n$, successful reordering, graph solve and equation-level residual multiplication preserve the $O(n^3+sn^2)$ scalar-core bound. This exact postprocessing count excludes algebraic bit cost, evaluator implementation cost beyond its declared unit budget, dense product-factor evaluation, and any additional dense residual multiplication. It is not a fixed-precision floating-point flop or structured backward-stability bound.

One dense Bartels–Stewart Lyapunov solve in its specified cubic branch costs $O(n^3)$; $J$ exact Newton-Kleinman policy evaluations therefore cost $O(m^3+Jn^3+J(n^2m+nm^2))$ for state dimension $n$ and input dimension $m$, charging one factorization of $R$ of order $m$ once. One SDA step costs $O(n^3)$, so $N$ exact steps cost $O(Nn^3)$.

Every computed candidate still requires its actual CARE/DARE residual and Hermitian symmetry defect. A DARE candidate also requires a positive lower bound for $R+B^*XB$; both equations require an independently certified closed-loop Hurwitz/Schur condition before the stabilizing branch is accepted. A computed QZ backward error for an unstructured nearby pencil does not certify nearby Hamiltonian/symplectic structure or positive $Q,R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Dense scalar arithmetic, finite Schur/QZ sweep budgets, dense direct factors and solves, and exact matrix dimensions.

[F1] [[alg-finite-budget-schur-qz-riccati-candidate-extraction]]: candidate extraction calls finite Schur/QZ reductions and exact stable-block reordering, solves $XU_1=U_2$, and reports actual Riccati residual, symmetry defect, positivity, and closed-loop stability data.

[F2] [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]]: Francis reduction first reduces to Hessenberg form and then performs bounded QR bulge-chasing sweeps.

[F3] [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]]: QZ iteration first reduces a regular pair to Hessenberg-triangular form and then performs bounded QZ sweeps.

[F4] [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]]: its cubic branch sets $N_A\le c_0m$ and $N_B\le c_0n$ for the two Schur reductions, then solves the resulting triangular Sylvester equation.

[F5] [[alg-finite-budget-newton-kleinman-policy-iteration]]: each exact Newton-Kleinman update performs one Lyapunov solve and one gain update.

[F6] [[alg-finite-budget-structure-preserving-doubling-for-dare]]: each SDA update solves with $I+G_jH_j$ and forms three dense matrix updates.

[F7] [[thm-computed-qz-pair-has-certified-backward-error]]: the QZ backward-error statement certifies the computed pair against an unstructured nearby pencil.

[F8] [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]]: the acceptance quantities are the CARE/DARE residuals, symmetry, DARE matrix $R+B^*XB$, and the corresponding closed-loop matrices.

[F9] [[alg-finite-budget-stable-block-reordering-for-schur-and-qz]]: the exact reordering has initial form-validation work, bounded-size local solves, whole-panel updates, and separate finite $K,W$ budgets.

[F10] [[thm-finite-budget-stable-block-reordering-correctness-and-status]]: each accepted adjacent inversion swap reduces the count by one and the exact factors transport existing unstructured residual norms.

[F11] [[thm-bartels-stewart-finite-status-and-local-pivot-uniqueness]]: the admitted finite solve terminates with a declared status and every successful local pivot is unique.

[A1] Dense reductions and equation solves use classical dense multiplication, factorization, and triangular solve costs. Reordering counts exact scalar primitives and declared evaluator units; algebraic bit cost, evaluator implementation cost, factor evaluation, and any uncounted enclosure work remain separate.

## Proof

1.1 In a Householder Hessenberg reduction, there are at most $n$ reflectors. At each stage a reflector updates a trailing block with at most $n^2$ entries using matrix-vector and rank-one operations, so the initialization costs $O(n^3)$. In a Francis or QZ bulge-chasing sweep, there are $O(n)$ rotations/reflections; each is applied to $O(n)$ entries in the active matrix and accumulated factor, hence a sweep costs $O(n^2)$. The finite budgets in [F2]–[F3] therefore give $O(n^3+sn^2)$ core work. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Dense LU factorization of $U_1$ costs $O(n^3)$; applying its factors to $n$ right-hand sides costs $O(n^3)$. The residual product $(XU_1-U_2)$ is also $O(n^3)$, yielding the candidate solve count in [F1]. In the Lyapunov branch, [F4] imposes $N_A,N_B\le c_0n$. By step 1.1, each of its two dense Schur reductions therefore costs $O(n^3)$; exact certificate checks and factor transformations are also $O(n^3)$. Triangular substitution for $n^2$ unknown entries with $O(n)$ work per entry costs $O(n^3)$, so one solve in this cubic branch costs $O(n^3)$. The fixed controller is bounded there; arbitrary-terminating-controller work is separate. [A1, F1, F4, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $d$ be the reduction order, $b$ its diagonal block count and $I$ its initial inversion count. The reordering validation scan costs $O(d^2)$. Each local system has order at most eight, and each exact factor update touches $O(d)$ panel entries, so $k$ attempts cost $O(d^2+kd)$ by [F9]. On success, [F10] gives $k=I\le b(b-1)/2\le d(d-1)/2$, so the worst-case reordering core is $O(d^3)$; this success path also requires $K\ge I$ and sufficient $W$ for the entire execution through its final ordering scan. For a Riccati matrix of order $2n$, combining reduction, reordering, graph solve and dense equation residual multiplication preserves $O(n^3+sn^2)$ scalar-core work. Exact algebraic bit cost, evaluator implementation, dense factor-product evaluation and any additional dense residual multiplication are separate costs. [A1, F1, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Each exact Newton-Kleinman pass has one Bartels–Stewart solve by [F5], costing $O(n^3)$ by step 2.1. Factorizing $R$ once costs $O(m^3)$. With $m$ controls, forming $B^*X$ and the gain uses $O(n^2m+m^2n)$ arithmetic including triangular solves with this pre-factored $R$; forming $K^*RK$ and $A-BK$ is bounded by the same $O(n^2m+nm^2)$ term. Summing over $J$ passes gives $O(m^3+Jn^3+J(n^2m+nm^2))$. Each SDA step uses one dense $n\times n$ solve and a fixed number of dense products, each $O(n^3)$; [F6] therefore gives $O(Nn^3)$ over $N$ steps. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A small backward error for a computed QZ pair, as supplied by [F7], is a statement about an unstructured nearby pencil. It contains no premise that the perturbation preserves Hamiltonian or symplectic block relations, nor that it preserves positive definiteness of $Q$ or $R$. Consequently acceptance must separately compute the equation residual and symmetry defect, check $R+B^*XB\succ0$ for DARE, and certify the closed-loop stability property in [F8]; [F1] explicitly reports these quantities. Neither ordering a computed form nor its unstructured backward error establishes a structured pencil perturbation or an equation-level stabilizing certificate. [F1, F7, F8, given, algebra] ∎

Forming a graph candidate by solving $XU_1=U_2$ with dense $n\times n$ factorization, $n$ right-hand sides, and residual multiplication costs $O(n^3)$.

After an order-$d$ reduction, finite stable-block reordering with $k$ actual attempts costs $O(d^2+kd)$ scalar operations. If the form has $b$ diagonal blocks and $I$ complementary-before-selected inversions, then $I\le b(b-1)/2$; successful ordering requires $K\ge I$ and enough scalar/evaluator budget $W$ for the entire execution, including validation, label and inversion scans, all $I$ swaps, and the final ordering scan. For a Riccati pencil or Hamiltonian with $d=2n$, successful reordering, graph solve and equation-level residual multiplication preserve the $O(n^3+sn^2)$ scalar-core bound. This exact postprocessing count excludes algebraic bit cost, evaluator implementation cost beyond its declared unit budget, dense product-factor evaluation, and any additional dense residual multiplication. It is not a fixed-precision floating-point flop or structured backward-stability bound.

One dense Bartels–Stewart Lyapunov solve in its specified cubic branch costs $O(n^3)$; $J$ exact Newton-Kleinman policy evaluations therefore cost $O(m^3+Jn^3+J(n^2m+nm^2))$ for state dimension $n$ and input dimension $m$, charging one factorization of $R$ of order $m$ once. One SDA step costs $O(n^3)$, so $N$ exact steps cost $O(Nn^3)$.

Every computed candidate still requires its actual CARE/DARE residual and Hermitian symmetry defect. A DARE candidate also requires a positive lower bound for $R+B^*XB$; both equations require an independently certified closed-loop Hurwitz/Schur condition before the stabilizing branch is accepted. ## Statement

Let $U^n$ be a scheme from
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], satisfying the full
invariant-interval CFL bound. For $k\in\mathbb R$ define
$$G_k(a,b):=F(a\vee k,b\vee k)-F(a\wedge k,b\wedge k),\qquad q_k(s):=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)(f(s)-f(k)),$$
where $q_k$ is the Kruzhkov entropy flux of
[[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]. Then $G_k(s,s)=q_k(s)$ for every $s\in I$,
and for every $j\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$,
$$|U_j^{n+1}-k|-|U_j^n-k|+\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr)\le0.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The full-line finite-volume recurrence with monotone consistent flux $F$, invariant interval $I=[a_-,a_+]$, the full invariant-interval CFL bound, and an arbitrary entropy level $k\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] The update is $U_j^{n+1}=H(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$; $H$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for $s\in I$ ([[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], [[lem-monotone-fv-update-preserves-range-and-tvd]]).

[F2] Consistency gives $F(s,s)=f(s)$, and the Kruzhkov flux is $q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)(f(s)-f(k))$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], [[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $s\ge k$, then $s\vee k=s$ and $s\wedge k=k$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(s)-f(k)=q_k(s)$. If $s<k$, then $s\vee k=k$ and $s\wedge k=s$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(k)-f(s)=q_k(s)$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 First suppose $k\in I$. Put $X=(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and let $X^+$ and $X^-$ be its coordinatewise maximum and minimum with $(k,k,k)$. Both triples lie in $I^3$. By [F1], the two numbers $H(X)$ and $H(k,k,k)=k$ lie between $H(X^-)$ and $H(X^+)$; therefore $|H(X)-k|\le H(X^+)-H(X^-).$ Expanding the definition of $H$, the right side is $|U_j^n-k|-\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr),$ which gives the claimed inequality after rearrangement. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If $k<a_-$, every state is above $k$ by the range assertion in [F1]. Then $|U_j^n-k|=U_j^n-k$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(a,b)-F(k,k)$ for state pairs; substituting the scheme recurrence makes the displayed left side zero. If $k>a_+$, every state is below $k$, so $|U_j^n-k|=k-U_j^n$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(k,k)-F(a,b)$; substitution again gives zero. The cases $k=a_-$ and $k=a_+$ are already covered by step 2.1. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U^n$ be a scheme from
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], satisfying the full
invariant-interval CFL bound. For $k\in\mathbb R$ define
$$G_k(a,b):=F(a\vee k,b\vee k)-F(a\wedge k,b\wedge k),\qquad q_k(s):=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)(f(s)-f(k)),$$
where $q_k$ is the Kruzhkov entropy flux of
[[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]. Then $G_k(s,s)=q_k(s)$ for every $s\in I$,
and for every $j\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$,
$$|U_j^{n+1}-k|-|U_j^n-k|+\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr)\le0.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The full-line finite-volume recurrence with monotone consistent flux $F$, invariant interval $I=[a_-,a_+]$, the full invariant-interval CFL bound, and an arbitrary entropy level $k\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] The update is $U_j^{n+1}=H(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$; $H$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing on $I^3$ and $H(s,s,s)=s$ for $s\in I$ ([[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], [[lem-monotone-fv-update-preserves-range-and-tvd]]).

[F2] Consistency gives $F(s,s)=f(s)$, and the Kruzhkov flux is $q_k(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s-k)(f(s)-f(k))$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$ ([[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], [[def-kruzhkov-entropy-solution]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $s\ge k$, then $s\vee k=s$ and $s\wedge k=k$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(s)-f(k)=q_k(s)$. If $s<k$, then $s\vee k=k$ and $s\wedge k=s$, so $G_k(s,s)=f(k)-f(s)=q_k(s)$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 First suppose $k\in I$. Put $X=(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)$ and let $X^+$ and $X^-$ be its coordinatewise maximum and minimum with $(k,k,k)$. Both triples lie in $I^3$. By [F1], the two numbers $H(X)$ and $H(k,k,k)=k$ lie between $H(X^-)$ and $H(X^+)$; therefore $|H(X)-k|\le H(X^+)-H(X^-).$ Expanding the definition of $H$, the right side is $|U_j^n-k|-\lambda\bigl(G_k(U_j^n,U_{j+1}^n)-G_k(U_{j-1}^n,U_j^n)\bigr),$ which gives the claimed inequality after rearrangement. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If $k<a_-$, every state is above $k$ by the range assertion in [F1]. Then $|U_j^n-k|=U_j^n-k$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(a,b)-F(k,k)$ for state pairs; substituting the scheme recurrence makes the displayed left side zero. If $k>a_+$, every state is below $k$, so $|U_j^n-k|=k-U_j^n$ and $G_k(a,b)=F(k,k)-F(a,b)$; substitution again gives zero. The cases $k=a_-$ and $k=a_+$ are already covered by step 2.1. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh, and consider $U_t+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\partial_{x_\ell}F_\ell(U)=0$ with state domain $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$. Assume a common convex entropy $\eta$ and, for each direction $\ell$, an entropy flux $q_\ell$ so that $(\eta,q_\ell)$ satisfies [[def-pe03-system-entropy-pair-and-potential]] for the directional flux $F_\ell$. Write $v=\nabla\eta$ and $\psi_\ell=v^TF_\ell-q_\ell$. For every direction, supply a symmetric consistent two-point flux $F_\ell^{ec}$ satisfying [[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]], namely
$$\bigl(v(U_R)-v(U_L)\bigr)^TF_\ell^{ec}(U_L,U_R)=\psi_\ell(U_R)-\psi_\ell(U_L).$$

On each cell use diagonal-norm SBP data from [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]. Put $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$; let $U_i^K\in\mathcal A$ be the nodal states; and let the face restrictions select paired face nodes with matching positive weights on the two incident cells. For an oriented interior face node with normal $n$ from the minus trace to the plus trace, set $F_n(U)=\sum_\ell n_\ell F_\ell(U)$ and $\psi_n(U)=\sum_\ell n_\ell\psi_\ell(U)$. Given any fixed coefficient $\alpha_{F,q}\ge0$, define the normal interface flux
$$\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*(U^-,U^+)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d n_\ell F_\ell^{ec}(U^-,U^+)-\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\bigl(v(U^+)-v(U^-)\bigr).$$
The coefficient is the same when the face orientation is reversed. Thus the flux is conservative and consistent, and its entropy contraction is
$$[v]^T\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*=[\psi_n]-\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\lVert[v]\rVert^2\le[\psi_n],$$
by the directional Tadmor identities in [[def-pe03-tadmor-entropy-conservative-flux]]. On physical boundary faces supply a consistent normal flux and require the boundary entropy contribution below to be nonnegative.

Write $\omega_{F,q}$ for the $q$th diagonal entry of $M_F$. Define the boundary entropy contribution
$$\mathcal B_h(t)=\sum_{F\subset\partial\Omega}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\bigl(v(U_{F,q})^T\widehat F_{n_F}^*-\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})\bigr).$$
The selected boundary flux is entropy admissible when $\mathcal B_h(t)\ge0$. The **flux-differencing SBP semidiscretization** on each element is
$$H_K\dot U^K+2\sum_{\ell=1}^d\bigl(Q_{K,\ell}\circ F_\ell^{ec}(U^K,U^K)\bigr)\mathbf1+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}\bigl(\widehat F_{n_{K,F}}^*-F_{n_{K,F}}(U_{K,F})\bigr)=0,$$
where $\circ$ is entrywise matrix multiplication and $F_\ell^{ec}(U^K,U^K)$ is the matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $F_\ell^{ec}(U_i^K,U_j^K)$. These are conditional method data: compatible SBP data and directional entropy-conservative fluxes are hypotheses, not asserted to exist for every mesh or entropy pair. The interior numerical flux is explicitly defined once those data and $\alpha_{F,q}$ are supplied. Curved elements are excluded.

## Statement

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$\nabla I_h^0f=I_h^1\nabla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{\nabla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice for the H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions; a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh, the local spaces and oriented degrees of freedom of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], a smooth scalar $f$, and smooth vector fields $u,v$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the distributional derivative uniqueness interfaces used to identify the global H(curl) and H(div) classes; no full Axiom of Choice is used. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The local edge basis is $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$, its six edge circulations are unisolvent, and the local face target is $RT_0(K)=\{a+cx\}$. ([[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], [[lem-na-nedelec-edge-unisolvence]])

[F2] Stokes on an oriented affine simplex identifies the integral of $d\eta$ with the signed sum of its face integrals. ([[lem-stokes-theorem-for-the-standard-simplex]])

[F3] Gauss–Green holds on each affine tetrahedron for a smooth vector field. ([[lem-affine-simplex-gauss-green-formula]])

[F4] Interior face orientations on a matching mesh are opposite and cancel in sums of oriented cell boundaries. ([[lem-oriented-facet-cancellation-on-matching-meshes]])

[F5] The affine covariant and contravariant Piola maps preserve oriented edge and face moments and commute with the corresponding weak differentials. ([[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]])

[F6] The integral of a derivative along a smooth segment is the difference of its endpoint values. ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]])

## Proof

1.1 For each cell $K$, define $I_K^0f$ by its four vertex values, $I_K^1u$ by its six edge circulations, $I_K^2v$ by its four face-normal fluxes, and $I_K^3g$ by its cell integral. The vertex basis $\lambda_i$ is dual to vertex evaluation. By [F1], the local edge-moment map is bijective, so any six prescribed edge values determine one local field; in particular they define $I_K^1u$. For $RT_0(K)$, the face flux map is injective: if all four fluxes of $q(x)=a+cx$ vanish, [F3] gives $3c|K|=\int_K\operatorname{div}q=0$, so $c=0$; then $a\cdot n_F=0$ for all four face normals. Three reference-tetrahedron face area vectors are linearly independent, and the invertible cofactor map in [F5] preserves this independence on $K$, so $a=0$. Since $RT_0(K)$ has dimension four, the four moments are bijective and any four prescribed values determine one field, defining $I_K^2v$. A constant is determined by its cell integral, so $I_K^3g$ is also unique. [F1, F3, F5, given, construct]

1.2 On a shared triangular face, the tangential trace of a local Nedelec field is a linear combination of the three Whitney edge traces on that face: a basis function from an edge containing the opposite vertex has zero tangential trace because the gradient of the opposite barycentric coordinate is normal to the face. The three face-edge circulations are unisolvent by the same endpoint calculation as [F1]. A global assignment gives the same oriented circulation from either incident tetrahedron, so the two tangential traces agree. Cellwise curl integration by parts, using [F3] on $u\times\varphi$ for a compactly supported smooth test $\varphi$, then cancels all interior face terms by [F4]; boundary terms vanish because $\varphi$ is compactly supported. Hence the assembled edge field has a distributional curl equal to its piecewise polynomial curl in $L^2$ and lies in the global $H(\operatorname{curl})$ space. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.3 The identity $\sum_{j\ne i}\phi_{ij}=-\nabla\lambda_i$ (where $\phi_{ji}:=-\phi_{ij}$) follows from $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ and $\sum_j\nabla\lambda_j=0$; hence $\nabla I_K^0f\in N_0(K)$. On an oriented edge $e=[x_i,x_j]$, [F6] gives $\int_e\nabla I_K^0f\cdot t_e\,ds=I_K^0f(x_j)-I_K^0f(x_i)=f(x_j)-f(x_i)=\int_e\nabla f\cdot t_e\,ds$. The two fields lie in the local Nedelec space, and [F1] makes the edge moments unisolvent, so $\nabla I_K^0f=I_K^1\nabla f$ on every cell. [F1, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Each $\operatorname{curl}\phi_{ij}=2\nabla\lambda_i\times\nabla\lambda_j$ is constant, so $\operatorname{curl}I_K^1u\in RT_0(K)$. For every oriented face $F$, Stokes [F2] gives $\int_F\operatorname{curl}(I_K^1u)\cdot n_F\,dS=\sum_{e\subset\partial F}\operatorname{sgn}(e,F)\int_e I_K^1u\cdot t_e\,ds=\int_F\operatorname{curl}u\cdot n_F\,dS$. The first equality uses the affine moment convention [F5]; the second uses the defining edge moments. Both curls are in $RT_0(K)$ and the four face moments are unisolvent by step 1.1, so $\operatorname{curl}I_K^1u=I_K^2\operatorname{curl}u$. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 On a tetrahedron $K$, Gauss–Green [F3] gives $\int_K\operatorname{div}(I_K^2v)\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\operatorname{sgn}(F,K)\int_F I_K^2v\cdot n_F\,dS=\int_K\operatorname{div}v\,dx$. Since $\operatorname{div}(a+cx)=3c$ is constant, equality of these cell integrals proves $\operatorname{div}I_K^2v=I_K^3\operatorname{div}v$ on $K$. More generally, every local RT0 normal trace is constant on a planar face because $x\cdot n_F$ is constant there; a shared oriented face moment therefore determines the same physical normal component from both cells. Summing cellwise Gauss–Green against a compact test function cancels interior terms by [F4], while boundary terms vanish, so the assembled face field has distributional divergence equal to its piecewise constant divergence in $L^2$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For any discrete $q_h\in W_h^0$, $u_h\in N_h^1$, or $v_h\in N_h^2$, its restriction to each cell is a polynomial and extends smoothly to a neighborhood of that cell. Apply the local identities in steps 1.3, 2.1 and 2.2 to these restrictions. The local interpolant is the identity on the corresponding finite-element input by the local moment unisolvence and construction in step 1.1, so the identities show $\nabla q_h|_K$, $\operatorname{curl}u_h|_K$, and $\operatorname{div}v_h|_K$ lie in their next local spaces. The edge moments of $\nabla q_h$ are endpoint differences of shared vertex values by step 1.3. The face fluxes of $\operatorname{curl}u_h$ are signed sums of the shared global edge values by step 2.1, so adjacent cells assign the same oriented flux to every shared face. The divergence target $N_h^3$ has only cellwise constant data and imposes no cross-cell matching. The assemblies in steps 1.2 and 2.2 give the required H(curl) and H(div) membership. Hence all three discrete differentials map between the stated global spaces, proving the subcomplex assertion. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$\nabla I_h^0f=I_h^1\nabla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{\nabla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice for the H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions; a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh, the local spaces and oriented degrees of freedom of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], a smooth scalar $f$, and smooth vector fields $u,v$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the distributional derivative uniqueness interfaces used to identify the global H(curl) and H(div) classes; no full Axiom of Choice is used. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The local edge basis is $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$, its six edge circulations are unisolvent, and the local face target is $RT_0(K)=\{a+cx\}$. ([[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], [[lem-na-nedelec-edge-unisolvence]])

[F2] Stokes on an oriented affine simplex identifies the integral of $d\eta$ with the signed sum of its face integrals. ([[lem-stokes-theorem-for-the-standard-simplex]])

[F3] Gauss–Green holds on each affine tetrahedron for a smooth vector field. ([[lem-affine-simplex-gauss-green-formula]])

[F4] Interior face orientations on a matching mesh are opposite and cancel in sums of oriented cell boundaries. ([[lem-oriented-facet-cancellation-on-matching-meshes]])

[F5] The affine covariant and contravariant Piola maps preserve oriented edge and face moments and commute with the corresponding weak differentials. ([[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]])

[F6] The integral of a derivative along a smooth segment is the difference of its endpoint values. ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]])

## Proof

1.1 For each cell $K$, define $I_K^0f$ by its four vertex values, $I_K^1u$ by its six edge circulations, $I_K^2v$ by its four face-normal fluxes, and $I_K^3g$ by its cell integral. The vertex basis $\lambda_i$ is dual to vertex evaluation. By [F1], the local edge-moment map is bijective, so any six prescribed edge values determine one local field; in particular they define $I_K^1u$. For $RT_0(K)$, the face flux map is injective: if all four fluxes of $q(x)=a+cx$ vanish, [F3] gives $3c|K|=\int_K\operatorname{div}q=0$, so $c=0$; then $a\cdot n_F=0$ for all four face normals. Three reference-tetrahedron face area vectors are linearly independent, and the invertible cofactor map in [F5] preserves this independence on $K$, so $a=0$. Since $RT_0(K)$ has dimension four, the four moments are bijective and any four prescribed values determine one field, defining $I_K^2v$. A constant is determined by its cell integral, so $I_K^3g$ is also unique. [F1, F3, F5, given, construct]

1.2 On a shared triangular face, the tangential trace of a local Nedelec field is a linear combination of the three Whitney edge traces on that face: a basis function from an edge containing the opposite vertex has zero tangential trace because the gradient of the opposite barycentric coordinate is normal to the face. The three face-edge circulations are unisolvent by the same endpoint calculation as [F1]. A global assignment gives the same oriented circulation from either incident tetrahedron, so the two tangential traces agree. Cellwise curl integration by parts, using [F3] on $u\times\varphi$ for a compactly supported smooth test $\varphi$, then cancels all interior face terms by [F4]; boundary terms vanish because $\varphi$ is compactly supported. The edge moments of $\nabla q_h$ are endpoint differences of shared vertex values by step 1.3. The face fluxes of $\operatorname{curl}u_h$ are signed sums of the shared global edge values by step 2.1, so adjacent cells assign the same oriented flux to every shared face. The divergence target $N_h^3$ has only cellwise constant data and imposes no cross-cell matching. The assemblies in steps 1.2 and 2.2 give the required H(curl) and H(div) membership. Hence all three discrete differentials map between the stated global spaces, proving the subcomplex assertion. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let f(y)=a+b·y be affine on R^d. Full-space smoothing by an admissible symmetric kernel reproduces f exactly: S_εf(x)=f(x) for every ε>0 and x∈R^d.

**Given:** An admissible kernel W, ε>0, a∈R, and b∈R^d.

[F3] [[lem-symmetric-kernel-moment-cancellation]]: ∫zW_ε(z)dz=0.

## Verification

1.1 Expand the affine function at x: f(x−z)=a+b·(x−z)=f(x)−b·z. [given, algebra]

Let f(y)=a+b·y be affine on R^d. Full-space smoothing by an admissible symmetric kernel reproduces f exactly: S_εf(x)=f(x) for every ε>0 and x∈R^d.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An admissible kernel W, ε>0, a∈R, and b∈R^d.

[F1] [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]]: S_εf(x)=∫f(x−z)W_ε(z)dz.

[F2] [[lem-scaled-kernel-moments-and-derivative-bounds]]: ∫W_ε=1.

[F3] [[lem-symmetric-kernel-moment-cancellation]]: ∫zW_ε(z)dz=0.

## Verification

1.1 Expand the affine function at x: f(x−z)=a+b·(x−z)=f(x)−b·z. [given, algebra]

2.1 Substitute this expansion into [F1]. The constant term integrates to f(x) by [F2], and the linear term vanishes by [F3]. Thus S_εf(x)=f(x). [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

For N=2 in [[def-regularized-conservative-sph-system]], write F_12 for the contribution of particle 2 to m_1v̇_1 and F_21 for the contribution of particle 1 to m_2v̇_2. These pair contributions are equal and opposite and act along the particle separation line.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two positions q_1,q_2 in R^d with positive masses and positive SPH densities.

[F1] [[def-regularized-conservative-sph-system]]: F_12=−m_1m_2(A_1+A_2)∇W_ε(q_1−q_2).

[F2] [[lem-sph-pair-forces-antisymmetric-and-central]]: F_21=−F_12 and F_12 is parallel to q_1−q_2.

## Verification

1.1 The two-particle acceleration equations contain precisely F_12 in the first momentum equation and F_21 in the second, by [F1]. [F1, given]

2.1 Applying [F2] gives F_12+F_21=0 and makes each force a scalar multiple of q_1−q_2; hence the pair exerts no net force or torque. [F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

In the Poisson setting of [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]],
$\|\cdot\|_{\sharp,h}$ is a norm on $X_h=H^1_0(\Omega)+V_h^{CR,0}$.
Its restriction to $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the gradient norm, equivalent to the
$H^1$ norm, and its restriction to $V_h^{CR,0}$ is a norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite matching mesh of a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $X_h$ and $\|\cdot\|_{\sharp,h}$ from [[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], and Countable Choice.

[F1] The expression is the sum of squared broken-gradient and scaled facet-jump terms; on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ all jumps vanish. ([[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], [[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]])

[F2] A zero-gradient $W^{1,2}$ function on a simplex is constant by its Poincare–Wirtinger inequality; shape-regular affine scaling transfers the inequality from the reference simplex. ([[thm-reference-simplex-poincare-wirtinger]], [[lem-shape-regular-affine-simplex-scaling]])

[F3] Interior points of a connected open domain can be joined by a polygonal path in the domain. ([[cor-components-of-open-subsets-of-rn-are-polygonally-connected]])

[F4] The gradient norm is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm on $H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([[lem-crouzeix-raviart-continuous-poincare]])

[F5] Every nonempty Euclidean ball has positive Lebesgue measure. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]])

[F6] A finite union of measurable null sets is null by finite subadditivity. ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]])

[F7] Cauchy--Schwarz in a real inner-product space gives $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, and expansion of $\|x+y\|^2$ then gives the triangle inequality for its induced norm. ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]])

## Proof
1.1 Let $z\in X_h$ and suppose $\|z\|_{\sharp,h}=0$. Each nonnegative term in the finite sum is zero, so $\nabla(z|_K)=0$ on every cell and every interior and boundary facet jump vanishes. By [F2], each restriction $z|_K$ is a constant $c_K$ almost everywhere. To see that the cell-adjacency graph is connected, choose interior points in any two cells and join them by a polygonal path in $\Omega$ using [F3]. Its compact image has positive distance from $\partial\Omega$. Subdivide its segments if necessary to obtain at least one intermediate vertex; perturb each intermediate vertex in a small open ball so all joining segments stay in $\Omega$. For a fixed endpoint $a$ off a mesh face $S$ of codimension at least two, candidate points in a bounded perturbation ball whose segment from $a$ meets $S$ lie in a truncated cone $\{a+t(s-a):s\in S,1\le t\le L\}$; $L<\infty$ because $a$ is a positive distance from the compact face and the candidate ball is bounded. If $S$ has dimension $k\le d-2$, cover the bounded parameter set $S\times[1,L]$ by $O(\delta^{-(k+1)})$ cubes of side $\delta$. The cone map is Lipschitz, so their images fit in $d$-cubes of side $C\delta$ with total volume $O(\delta^{d-k-1})\to0$. Bounded portions of facet hyperplanes are also null by the same covering count with $k=d-1$. Thus all forbidden sets are measurable null sets, and [F6] makes each finite union null. By [F5], a perturbation ball has positive measure and so contains a point outside that union. Choose the intermediate vertices successively outside the finitely many cones from the previous vertex and facet hyperplanes; for the last vertex also avoid the cones from the fixed endpoint at the end of the path. No segment meets the codimension-at-least-two skeleton or lies in a facet hyperplane, so cell transitions occur only through relative interiors of whole facets. When $d=1$, the mesh faces are endpoints and each crossing is itself a whole facet. The crossings give a cell-adjacency chain. Zero interior jumps therefore make all constants $c_K$ equal, while a zero boundary-facet jump makes the constant zero. Every cell is connected to that boundary cell, so $z=0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. Thus the kernel is trivial. [F2, F3, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Map $z\in X_h$ to the finite direct sum $Y=\bigoplus_K L^2(K;\mathbb R^d)\oplus\bigoplus_F L^2(F)$ by $Jz=((\nabla z|_K)_K,(h_F^{-1/2}[z]_F)_F)$. The sum of the component integral pairings is an inner product on $Y$, and its induced norm satisfies $\|Jz\|_Y=\|z\|_{\sharp,h}$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] and expansion of the squared norm give the triangle inequality; step 1.1 shows $J$ is injective, proving positive definiteness on $X_h$. If $z=u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, its interior and boundary jumps vanish by the local trace theorem, so the expression equals $\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$, equivalent to the $H^1$ norm by [F4]. Finally, on the finite-dimensional space $V_h^{CR,0}$ the restriction is an inner-product norm; in its explicit face basis its Gram matrix is positive definite, so that norm is equivalent to the Euclidean coefficient norm and is complete. Thus $V_h^{CR,0}$ is Hilbert in the comparison norm. [F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

[F1] The expression is the sum of squared broken-gradient and scaled facet-jump terms; on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ all jumps vanish. ([[def-crouzeix-raviart-poisson-method]], [[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]])

[F2] A zero-gradient $W^{1,2}$ function on a simplex is constant by its Poincare–Wirtinger inequality; shape-regular affine scaling transfers the inequality from the reference simplex. ([[thm-reference-simplex-poincare-wirtinger]], [[lem-shape-regular-affine-simplex-scaling]])

[F3] Interior points of a connected open domain can be joined by a polygonal path in the domain. ([[cor-components-of-open-subsets-of-rn-are-polygonally-connected]])

[F4] The gradient norm is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm on $H^1_0(\Omega)$. ([[lem-crouzeix-raviart-continuous-poincare]])

[F5] Every nonempty Euclidean ball has positive Lebesgue measure. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]])

[F6] A finite union of measurable null sets is null by finite subadditivity. ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]])

[F7] Cauchy--Schwarz in a real inner-product space gives $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, and expansion of $\|x+y\|^2$ then gives the triangle inequality for its induced norm. ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]])

1.1 Let $z\in X_h$ and suppose $\|z\|_{\sharp,h}=0$. Each nonnegative term in the finite sum is zero, so $\nabla(z|_K)=0$ on every cell and every interior and boundary facet jump vanishes. To see that the cell-adjacency graph is connected, choose interior points in any two cells and join them by a polygonal path in $\Omega$ using [F3]. Its compact image has positive distance from $\partial\Omega$. Subdivide its segments if necessary to obtain at least one intermediate vertex; perturb each intermediate vertex in a small open ball so all joining segments stay in $\Omega$. For a fixed endpoint $a$ off a mesh face $S$ of codimension at least two, candidate points in a bounded perturbation ball whose segment from $a$ meets $S$ lie in a truncated cone $\{a+t(s-a):s\in S,1\le t\le L\}$; $L<\infty$ because $a$ is a positive distance from the compact face and the candidate ball is bounded. If $S$ has dimension $k\le d-2$, cover the bounded parameter set $S\times[1,L]$ by $O(\delta^{-(k+1)})$ cubes of side $\delta$. The cone map is Lipschitz, so their images fit in $d$-cubes of side $C\delta$ with total volume $O(\delta^{d-k-1})\to0$. Bounded portions of facet hyperplanes are also null by the same covering count with $k=d-1$. Thus all forbidden sets are measurable null sets, and [F6] makes each finite union null. By [F5], a perturbation ball has positive measure and so contains a point outside that union. Choose the intermediate vertices successively outside the finitely many cones from the previous vertex and facet hyperplanes; for the last vertex also avoid the cones from the fixed endpoint at the end of the path. No segment meets the codimension-at-least-two skeleton or lies in a facet hyperplane, so cell transitions occur only through relative interiors of whole facets. Zero interior jumps therefore make all constants $c_K$ equal, while a zero boundary-facet jump makes the constant zero. Every cell is connected to that boundary cell, so $z=0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. Thus $V_h^{CR,0}$ is Hilbert in the comparison norm. [F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. If $\rho:=\|K_k\|_{L^2\to L^2}<1$, then for every $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ the equation $u=f+K_ku$ has a unique solution. For each integer $m\ge0$, define the Born partial sum $u_m:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}K_k^jf$. Then
$$\|u-u_m\|_2\le\frac{\rho^{m+1}}{1-\rho}\|f\|_2.$$
No compactness, analytic continuation, or physical uniqueness hypothesis is used in this small-norm branch.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $f\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$, and $K_k$ with operator norm $\rho<1$.

[F1] $K_k$ is a bounded linear operator on complex $L^2(D)$ ([[lem-volume-integral-operator-well-defined-and-bounded]]).

[F2] Complex $L^2(D)$ is complete under Countable Choice ([[thm-complex-lp-completeness-and-almost-everywhere-subsequences]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F3] For every integer $j\ge0$, $\|K_k^jf\|_2\le\rho^j\|f\|_2$, by repeated application of the operator norm inequality in [F1].

## Proof

**Given:** The data of the Statement, with $\rho=\|K_k\|<1$.

1.1 Define $u_N:=\sum_{j=0}^{N}K_k^jf$. For $M>N$, the triangle inequality and [F3] give $\|u_M-u_N\|_2\le\|f\|_2\sum_{j=N+1}^{M}\rho^j\le\|f\|_2\rho^{N+1}/(1-\rho)$. This tends to zero as $N\to\infty$, so $(u_N)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $u\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ by [F2]. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Finite telescoping gives $(I-K_k)u_N=f-K_k^{N+1}f$. By [F3], $\|K_k^{N+1}f\|_2\le\rho^{N+1}\|f\|_2\to0$; boundedness in [F1] lets $K_ku_N\to K_ku$. Taking limits yields $(I-K_k)u=f$. If $(I-K_k)v=0$, then $\|v\|_2=\|K_kv\|_2\le\rho\|v\|_2$, and $\rho<1$ forces $v=0$, so this solution is unique. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 With $m$ fixed, [F3] and the geometric-series identity give $\|u-u_m\|_2\le\sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty}\|K_k^jf\|_2\le\|f\|_2\sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty}\rho^j=\rho^{m+1}\|f\|_2/(1-\rho)$. The argument includes $\rho=0$ and $f=0$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Use $\epsilon=b=1$, $f=1$, homogeneous endpoint values, and one interior P1 degree of freedom on the two-cell mesh $h=1/2$. Replace the exact parameter $\tau$ by the deliberately oversized value $\widetilde\tau=M\tau$, $M>0$. The discrete midpoint value tends to zero as $M\to\infty$, while the exact midpoint value is fixed and positive.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-dimensional SUPG form, the two-cell homogeneous P1 space, $\epsilon=b=1$, $f=1$, and the modified parameter $\widetilde\tau=M\tau$.

[F1] [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]: the continuous problem is $-u''+u'=1$ on $(0,1)$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$.

[F2] [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]]: the stabilized diffusion coefficient in the P1 bilinear form is $\epsilon+\widetilde\tau b^2$, and the stabilization load is $\sum_K\widetilde\tau(f,b\phi')_K$.

[F3] [[lem-supg-one-dimensional-optimal-parameter]]: the reference parameter $\tau$ is strictly positive.

## Verification

1.1 The function $u(x)=x-(e^x-1)/(e-1)$ satisfies the endpoint conditions. Its derivatives are $u'=1-e^x/(e-1)$ and $u''=-e^x/(e-1)$, so $-u''+u'=1$. Hence $u(1/2)=u_*:=1/2-1/(\sqrt e+1)>0$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $\phi$ be the midpoint hat function and $U$ its coefficient. Its derivative is $2$ on the left cell and $-2$ on the right. Thus $\int_0^1|\phi'|^2dx=4$, $\int_0^1\phi'\phi\,dx=\frac12[\phi^2]_0^1=0$, and $\int_0^1\phi\,dx=1/2$. Also $\int_0^1\phi'\,dx=\phi(1)-\phi(0)=0$, so the stabilization load vanishes. The single discrete equation is therefore $4(1+M\tau)U=1/2$, so $U=1/[8(1+M\tau)]$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\tau>0$ by [F3], $U\to0$ as $M\to\infty$, whereas the exact value $u_*>0$ from step 1.1 is fixed. In particular, every $M$ satisfying $M\tau>1/(4u_*)-1$ gives $U<u_*/2$. Oversizing the parameter can therefore smear this discrete solution. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the one-dimensional model of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]] with homogeneous data $g_0=g_1=0$, and the form of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]]. Let $u\in C^2([0,1])$ solve $-\epsilon u''+bu'=f$ with $u(0)=u(1)=0$. Then $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ for every $v_h\in V_h$. For every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$a_h(v_h,v_h)=\epsilon\|v_h'\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2+\tau b^2\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\|v_h'\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$$
The right-hand side is a squared norm on $V_h$. Consequently the finite-dimensional SUPG system has a unique solution.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A uniform interval partition, $\epsilon>0$, $b\ne0$, $f\in C([0,1])$, the homogeneous problem above, and the SUPG form and parameter.

[F1] [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]: $V_h$ consists of continuous piecewise-affine functions vanishing at both endpoints; the exact solution satisfies $-\epsilon u''+bu'=f$.

[F2] [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]]: $a_h(w,v_h)$ pairs $-\epsilon w''+bw'$ against $\tau b v_h'$ cellwise and $F_h$ pairs $f$ against the same test perturbation; for P1 $w_h$, $w_h''=0$.

[F3] [[lem-supg-one-dimensional-optimal-parameter]]: $\tau>0$ for $\epsilon>0$, $b\ne0$, and $h>0$.

## Proof

1.1 For $v_h\in V_h$, continuity and piecewise absolute continuity give $\int_0^1bv_h'v_h\,dx=\frac b2\sum_K[v_h^2]_{\partial K}=\frac b2(v_h(1)^2-v_h(0)^2)=0$. The endpoint values vanish by [F1]. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Integration by parts, with $v_h(0)=v_h(1)=0$, gives $\epsilon(u',v_h')+(bu',v_h)=(-\epsilon u''+bu',v_h)=(f,v_h)$. The stabilization contribution to $a_h(u,v_h)$ is $\sum_K\tau(-\epsilon u''+bu',bv_h')_K$, which equals $\sum_K\tau(f,bv_h')_K$ by the strong equation. This is exactly the stabilization contribution to $F_h$, so $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Substituting step 1.1 into [F2] with $w_h=v_h$ yields the displayed identity. Its right side is nonnegative by [F3] and $\epsilon>0$. If it is zero, then $v_h'=0$ on every cell; continuity makes $v_h$ constant on $[0,1]$, and its zero endpoints force $v_h=0$. Hence this quadratic form is a norm squared. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In a basis of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$, the discrete form defines a square linear map $V_h\to V_h^*$. If a vector is in its kernel, testing with that vector and using step 2.1 gives that it is zero. Thus the map is injective, hence bijective in finite equal dimensions, so each discrete load has exactly one solution. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Subtracting the discrete equation from the consistency identity in step 1.2 gives $a_h(u-u_h,v_h)=0$ for every $v_h\in V_h$; the solution exists by step 3.1. [step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d\to R$ have bounded spatial derivatives through order two, with $R$ a compact rectangle. Let $F\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of $R$, and let $\mathcal A_h=-D A_h^{\rm per}$ be the periodic-grid diffusion generator from [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]. Define $F_h(P_hu)=P_h(F(u))$ pointwise. Then
$$\sup_{0<h_j\le1,\,0\le t\le T}\left\|\mathcal A_hF_h(P_hu(t))-DF(P_hu(t))\mathcal A_hP_hu(t)\right\|_\infty\le C_{\rm com}<\infty,$$
where $C_{\rm com}$ depends only on the dimension, $D$, the suprema of $D^2u$, $DF$, $D^2F$, and the compact state rectangle, not on the mesh widths. This is the finite-grid commutator used in the first-order split-error proof; it is not a claim for arbitrary meshes or unbounded operators.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The periodic uniform grid, a diagonal nonnegative diffusion matrix, $u$ with bounded spatial derivatives through order two, and $F\in C^2$ on a neighborhood of the compact range of $u$.

[F1] [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]: $\mathcal A_h=-D A_h^{\rm per}$ and each coordinate of $A_h^{\rm per}$ is a centered second difference divided by $h_j^2$.

[F2] [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]]: $F$ is defined on an open neighborhood of $R$; the additional $C^2$ assumption is in the Statement.

[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: if $G$ is differentiable on a compact interval, including its one-sided endpoint derivatives, and $G'$ is Darboux integrable there, then $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous scalar function on a compact interval is bounded and Darboux integrable.

[F5] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: if a scalar function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior, its endpoint difference equals an interior derivative times the interval length.

[F6] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]: a differentiable scalar function is continuous at each point of differentiability; in particular, an everywhere existing second derivative makes the first derivative continuous on each coordinate interval.

[A1] The range of $u$ lies in a compact rectangle $R$ and the displayed derivatives are uniformly bounded on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T_L^d$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $w$ be a twice differentiable scalar function on a coordinate lift with bounded $w''$. By [F6], $w'$ is continuous; hence $s\mapsto w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)$ is continuous and integrable on $[0,h]$ by [F4]. Apply [F3] to the differentiable function $s\mapsto w(x+s)+w(x-s)-2w(x)$, whose endpoint derivatives are the corresponding one-sided restrictions. This gives $$w(x+h)-2w(x)+w(x-h)=\int_0^h\bigl(w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)\bigr)\,ds.$$ For $s>0$, [F5] applied to $w'$ on $[x-s,x+s]$ gives $|w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)|\le2s\|w''\|_\infty$; at $s=0$ this also holds. Integrating yields $|w(x+h)-2w(x)+w(x-h)|\le h^2\|w''\|_\infty$. Thus the centered second difference divided by $h^2$ has the same mesh-independent bound. Only the continuous first derivative was integrated; integrability or continuity of $w''$ is not assumed. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]


2.1 Fix a component $i$ and a spatial direction $j$. The chain rule first gives $\partial_j(F_i(u))=\sum_k\partial_kF_i(u)\,\partial_ju_k$. Applying the product rule to each summand and the chain rule to $\partial_kF_i(u)$ gives $$\partial_{jj}(F_i(u))=\sum_k\partial_kF_i(u)\,\partial_{jj}u_k+\sum_{k,\ell}\partial_{k\ell}F_i(u)(\partial_ju_k)(\partial_ju_\ell).$$ These are pointwise identities under the stated second-order spatial differentiability of $u$ and $F\in C^2$ near its range. To express the bound using only the quantities listed in the Statement, let $w_k=\sup_R z_k-\inf_R z_k$ and $H_{kj}=\|\partial_{jj}u_k\|_\infty$. For $g(s)=u_k(x+se_j,t)$ on the periodic lift, $g'$ is continuous by [F6], and $r\mapsto g'(r)-g'(0)$ is integrable on $[0,s]$ by [F4]. Apply [F3] to $r\mapsto g(r)-g(0)-rg'(0)$ to get $g(s)-g(0)-sg'(0)=\int_0^s(g'(r)-g'(0))\,dr$. By [F5] on $g'$, $|g'(r)-g'(0)|\le rH_{kj}$ for $0\le r\le s$. The remainder is therefore bounded by $s^2H_{kj}/2$. Since $|g(s)-g(0)|\le w_k$, this yields, for every $s>0$, $$s|\partial_ju_k(x,t)|\le w_k+\frac{s^2}{2}H_{kj}.$$ If $w_kH_{kj}>0$, choose $s=\sqrt{2w_k/H_{kj}}$ to obtain $|\partial_ju_k|\le\sqrt{2w_kH_{kj}}$. If $H_{kj}=0$, the same inequality for every $s$ gives $\partial_ju_k=0$; if $w_k=0$, the component is constant and the same conclusion holds. Therefore the displayed chain-rule terms are uniformly bounded in terms of $R$, $D^2u$, $DF$, and $D^2F$, as asserted. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]


3.1 In each component, $\mathcal A_hF_h(P_hu)$ is a finite sum of $d_i$ times the centered second differences of $F_i\circ u$, while $DF(P_hu)\mathcal A_hP_hu$ is the finite sum of $\partial_kF_i(u)d_k$ times the centered second differences of $u_k$. Step 1.1 bounds each difference uniformly, and step 2.1 bounds every coefficient. There are only $d m^2$ terms and $D$ is fixed, so their sum is bounded by a constant independent of all $h_j$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ have a fixed finite matching affine tensor-box mesh with cell degrees $p_K\ge1$, and let $V_p$ be its trace-matching hp space. On $V=H^1(\Omega)$ use $a(v,w)=\int_\Omega(\nabla v\cdot\nabla w+vw)$ and a bounded load $F$. Let $u$ solve the exact variational problem and let $u_p\in V_p$ solve the cellwise GLL quadrature problem with the same load exactly restricted to $V_p$. Define the form defect $\delta_{a,p}$ by [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. Then
$$\|u-u_p\|_{H^1(\Omega)} \le \inf_{v_p\in V_p}\bigl(2\|u-v_p\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+\delta_{a,p}(v_p)\bigr).$$
The stability factor is uniform in all cell degrees. The defect is retained as stated; no aliasing or p-decay estimate is asserted, and GLL assembly is not identified with exact Galerkin assembly.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the finite matching affine tensor-box mesh and $p_K\ge1$; exact $a,F,u$; the GLL form $a_p$; and its discrete solution $u_p$.

[F1] [[lem-variable-degree-polynomial-spaces-are-h1-conforming]]: the trace-matching hp space is finite-dimensional and contained in $H^1(\Omega)$.

[F2] [[thm-hp-gll-top-mode-and-puniform-energy-equivalence]]: on each affine box the GLL quadrature H1 form is bounded above by $3^d$ times and below by $1$ times the exact local H1 form, uniformly in its degree.

[F3] [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]: $\delta_{a,p}(v_p)=\sup_{w_p\ne0}|a(v_p,w_p)-a_p(v_p,w_p)|/\|w_p\|_{H^1}$, while the load defect is defined analogously.

[F4] [[thm-first-strang-lemma-for-conforming-perturbed-galerkin]]: under Countable Choice, a coercive exact and discrete form on a finite-dimensional conforming subspace satisfy the first Strang estimate with the form and load defects from [F3].

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: a positive weighted finite sum obeys Cauchy–Schwarz.

## Proof

1.1 Sum [F2] over cells. For every $v_p\in V_p$, $a(v_p,v_p)=\|v_p\|_{H^1}^2$ and $a_p(v_p,v_p)\ge\|v_p\|_{H^1}^2$; Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] for the positive quadrature weights gives $|a_p(v_p,w_p)|\le3^d\|v_p\|_{H^1}\|w_p\|_{H^1}$. Thus the discrete form is bounded and coercive with $\alpha_p\ge1$, and the exact form has $M=1$. The exact load is unchanged on $V_p$, so $\delta_{F,p}=0$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F4] with $V=H^1(\Omega)$, the finite-dimensional conforming subspace from [F1], exact bounded coercive form $a$, GLL form $a_p$, and the restricted load. Its bound is $\inf_{v_p\in V_p}((1+M/\alpha_p)\|u-v_p\|+(\delta_{a,p}(v_p)+\delta_{F,p})/\alpha_p)$. Substituting $M=1$, $\alpha_p\ge1$, and $\delta_{F,p}=0$ from step 1.1 yields the stated inequality. Countable Choice is the only axiom used by [F4]. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

Let $u$ solve the exact variational problem and let $u_p\in V_p$ solve the cellwise GLL quadrature problem with the same load exactly restricted to $V_p$. $$\|u-u_p\|_{H^1(\Omega)} \le \inf_{v_p\in V_p}\bigl(2\|u-v_p\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+\delta_{a,p}(v_p)\bigr).$$
