## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a conforming affine simplicial mesh, and piecewise RT0 vector polynomials with the stated facet flux conditions.

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited through the Sobolev trace and density interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] RT0 on a cell is $\mathbb P_0(K)^d+x\mathbb P_0(K)$, and each simplex has $d+1$ facets. ([[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]])

[F2] Piola preserves RT0 and its divergence and oriented facet flux. ([[lem-na-piola-preserves-rt-bdm-spaces]], [[lem-na-piola-divergence-and-flux-identities]])

[F3] On a smooth field on a simplex, the integral of its divergence equals the sum of its outward facet fluxes. ([[lem-affine-simplex-gauss-green-formula]])

[F4] H1 functions on a cell have $L^2$ facet traces; the traces from adjacent cells agree for a global H1 function. ([[lem-na-simplex-h1-facet-trace-bound]], [[lem-na-h1-interior-facet-traces-agree]])

[F5] Smooth-neighborhood functions are dense in H1 of each cell. ([[lem-na-smooth-neighborhood-dense-in-h1-simplex]])

[F6] The weak normal trace on the global domain is Green duality, and H0(div) is its zero kernel. ([[lem-na-hdiv-weak-normal-trace]], [[def-na-h0div-space]])

[F7] The regular-distribution map is injective on $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ modulo almost-everywhere equality under Countable Choice. An $L^2$ function is locally integrable: on compact $C$, finite Lebesgue measure and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_2$. ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]])

## Proof

1.1 On the reference simplex $\widehat S_d=\{x_i>0,\sum_i x_i<1\}$, each coordinate facet has outward normal $-e_i$ and area $1/(d-1)!$, while the top facet has outward normal $(1,\ldots,1)/\sqrt d$ and area $\sqrt d/(d-1)!$. For $\widehat v=a+cx$, the constant-vector facet fluxes sum to zero by [F3], and the flux sum of $cx$ is $c/(d-1)!=dc|\widehat S_d|$. If all facet fluxes vanish then $c=0$; the coordinate-facet fluxes then force each $a_i=0$. The flux map is injective between spaces of dimension $d+1$, hence bijective. [A1, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For any physical simplex, [F2] transports the reference flux degrees of freedom bijectively, so the same unisolvence holds. On each facet, $(a+cx)\cdot n$ is constant because $x\cdot n$ is constant on its supporting hyperplane; equal integrated fluxes therefore give equal normal components. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field with matching shared-facet fluxes. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, apply [F3] to $\phi v$ cellwise and sum: interior facet terms cancel by step 2.1 and the common value of $\phi$, and boundary terms vanish because $\phi$ is compactly supported. Thus $\int_Dv\cdot\nabla\phi=-\sum_K\int_K(\operatorname{div}v)\phi$. The cellwise divergence is constant and in $L^2$, so $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$ by definition. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Conversely, let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field in H(div), with global $L^2$ divergence $g$. For every test supported in one cell, the global distributional identity and cellwise Gauss–Green give zero pairing with $g$ minus that cell's polynomial divergence. This difference is in $L^2(K)$ and hence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(K)$ by [F7]; extending from real to complex tests by linearity, injectivity [F7] makes the difference zero almost everywhere on the cell. For arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, summing cellwise Green formulas and comparing with the global distributional identity yields $\sum_{F=K^+\cap K^-\,\mathrm{interior}}\int_F\phi(v_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+v_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})=0$. Each normal sum is constant on its facet. If one were nonzero, choose a nonnegative smooth test supported in a small ball around a relative-interior point of that facet, meeting no other facet, and positive on a subpatch; the sum would be a nonzero constant times a positive surface integral, a contradiction. Hence all interior fluxes match. [A1, F3, F7, step 2.1, construct, contradiction]

4.1 Suppose the interior fluxes match. For $w\in H^1(D)$, approximate each restriction $w|_K$ in H1 by smooth-neighborhood functions using [F5]. The trace bound [F4] and volume convergence pass cellwise Gauss–Green to each restriction. Interior traces of $w$ agree by [F4], and the normal components of $v$ agree by step 2.1, so interior terms cancel. If $c_F$ denotes the constant outward normal component on a boundary facet $F$, the resulting identity is $\int_D(v\cdot\nabla w+\operatorname{div}v\,w)=\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw$. By [F6] this is the weak normal-trace functional; in particular, if every boundary flux is zero then $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$. [A1, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Conversely, if $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, its zero trace and the identity in step 4.1 give $\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw=0$ for every $w\in H^1(D)$. For any selected boundary facet, choose a smooth function on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in a small ball about a relative-interior point of that facet, positive on a subpatch, and meeting no other boundary facet; its restriction lies in $H^1(D)$. The sum then reduces to the selected $c_F$ times a positive surface integral, so $c_F=0$. Thus every boundary facet flux vanishes. [A1, F4, F6, step 3.2, step 4.1, construct, contradiction] ∎

## Statement

In the Countable Choice branch of [[def-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection]], the equation defining $R_hu$ has a unique solution for each $u\in V$. Moreover, with $\|v\|_{a_+}^2=a_+(v,v)$,
$$\|u-R_hu\|_{a_+}\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_{a_+}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite-dimensional real edge space and symmetric form $a_+$ from [[def-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection]], with uniformly positive definite $\epsilon$ and $\mu^{-1}$.

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited from the H(div) and affine Piola definitions that supply the FE spaces; the local linear-algebra argument below uses only the given finite space. ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection]])

[F1] The mass form $m$ and curl form $a$ are symmetric, and their sum satisfies $a_+(v,v)\ge c(\|v\|_{L^2}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_{L^2}^2)$ for some $c>0$. ([[def-maxwell-edge-ritz-projection]])

## Proof


1.1 By [F1], the Gram matrix of $a_+$ in any basis of the finite-dimensional $V_h$ is symmetric positive definite. Hence its kernel is zero and it is invertible, so the linear system defining $R_hu$ has exactly one solution. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Subtracting the defining equation from itself gives $a_+(u-R_hu,v_h)=0$ for every $v_h\in V_h$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For arbitrary $w_h\in V_h$, write $u-w_h=(u-R_hu)+(R_hu-w_h)$. The second summand lies in $V_h$, so [step 1.2] makes the cross term zero in the $a_+$ inner product. Thus $\|u-w_h\|_{a_+}^2=\|u-R_hu\|_{a_+}^2+\|R_hu-w_h\|_{a_+}^2\ge\|u-R_hu\|_{a_+}^2$. Taking the infimum proves the claim. [A1, F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice only as inherited from the real $H(\operatorname{div})$/Piola finite-element space interfaces in [[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]]. For the lossless source-free semidiscretization
$$M_e\dot e-C^TM_b b=0,\qquad \dot b+Ce=0,$$
the weighted energy
$$\mathcal H_h(t)=\frac12\|e(t)\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b(t)\|_{M_b}^2$$
is constant in time. The local matrix calculation uses no further choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The finite-dimensional semidiscrete fields, symmetric positive definite matrices, and the source-free equations above.

[A1] The Countable Choice Axiom is the principle that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; it is included only because the imported FE-space and Piola definitions declare it. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] $M_e,M_b$ are symmetric positive definite and the semidiscrete equations are $M_e\dot e=C^TM_b b$ and $M_b\dot b=-M_bCe$. ([[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]])

## Statement

For a sequence of diagonal-diffusion grid schemes satisfying the hypotheses
of [[thm-na-diagonal-diffusion-scheme-half-relaxed-limits]], suppose in
addition that the exact periodic Cauchy problem
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]] has a comparison
principle for bounded upper semicontinuous subsolutions and bounded lower
semicontinuous supersolutions with ordered relaxed initial traces. Then the
upper and lower half-relaxed limits coincide, define the unique bounded
continuous viscosity solution, and the spatially interpolated numerical
solutions converge locally uniformly on $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$ to it.
This corollary is conditional on the stated second-order comparison property;
it does not supply or assert that property.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The half-relaxed stability statement and the comparison hypothesis
in the corollary.

[F1] The upper limit is a bounded USC subsolution and the lower limit is a
bounded LSC supersolution with the same initial data, and
$\underline U\le\overline U$
([[thm-na-diagonal-diffusion-scheme-half-relaxed-limits]]).

[A1] The stated comparison principle applies to this periodic coefficient
class for the bounded semicontinuous sub- and supersolutions in [F1], with
their relaxed initial ordering. This is an explicit conditional hypothesis,
not a result proved on this page
([[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]],
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]]).

[F2] The set definitions of the relaxed limits imply that if both envelopes
equal a continuous function on a compact set, then a finite subcover of
nearby upper and lower bounds proves uniform convergence there
([[def-half-relaxed-limits]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

## Proof

1.1 Apply [A1] to the upper subsolution and lower supersolution supplied by [F1]. Their common initial trace gives the required ordering, hence $\overline U\le\underline U$. Together with the reverse inequality in [F1], this proves equality. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 The common function is both upper and lower semicontinuous by [F1], hence continuous. It is both a viscosity subsolution and supersolution, so is a viscosity solution with the prescribed initial data. Comparison in [A1] implies uniqueness. [A1, F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix $T'<T$ and let $K=[0,1]^d\times[0,T']$ in the periodic lift; this box is compact by Heine--Borel. Write $u$ for the common limit from step 2.1 and fix $\varepsilon>0$. For $z\in K$ and rational $q>0$, include $B(z,q/2)$ in a family when for every integer $k$ with $1/k<q$ and every $y$ with $|y-z|<q$, $|V_k(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$, and continuity gives $|u(y)-u(z)|<\varepsilon/3$. The set definitions in [F2] guarantee that these balls cover $K$: each point has a positive real radius, and a smaller rational radius works. The family consists of all qualifying pairs, so no radius is selected point by point. By [F2], a finite subcover exists; take the least of its finitely many rational radii. The triangle inequality then gives $|V_k(y)-u(y)|<2\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$ uniformly on $K$ for all sufficiently large $k$. This proves uniform convergence on the fundamental box through $T'$, hence on the torus and every compact subset of $\mathbb T^d\times[0,T)$. Thus the extensions converge locally uniformly. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For the square sites $A=(0,0),B=(1,0),C=(1,1),D=(0,1)$ with identifiers $1,2,3,4$ and zero weights, the unperturbed lifts are coplanar. In the four-site universe the perturbation $h_i=\|p_i\|^2+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}}$ selects diagonal $BD$. Adding three synthetic identifiers below these four sites multiplies all four perturbation exponents by $8$, so the algorithm's augmented universe selects the same diagonal. Both selected triangles are weakly empty in the original, unperturbed sense.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The four indexed sites and the fixed-universe lexicographic height rule.

[F1] [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]: the four stable identifiers are distinct, and absent weights are zero.

[F2] [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]]: rank $0,1,2,3$ receive height perturbations $\varepsilon,\varepsilon^2,\varepsilon^4,\varepsilon^8$, respectively.

[F3] [[thm-lexicographic-lift-tie-break-consistent]]: the first nonzero coefficient decides the one coherent formal lifted configuration.

[F4] [[def-planar-delaunay-voronoi-structures]]: a triangle is weakly empty-circle if no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk.

[F5] [[thm-incremental-planar-delaunay-correctness-and-termination]]: the fixed formal lift selects a terminating empty-circle triangulation.

[A1] The square is listed counterclockwise, all four weights are zero, and the four-site hand calculation uses exactly the universe $U=\{A,B,C,D\}$.

## Proof

1.1 The unperturbed heights are $0,1,2,1$. Each is $x+y$ at its site, so the four lifted points lie in the plane $z=x+y$. [given, A1, algebra]

1.2 All four original sites lie on the circle centered at $(1/2,1/2)$ with radius squared $1/2$. No other sites are present, so neither selected triangle has a site strictly inside its circumdisk. They are weakly empty by [F4]. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 With the perturbation from [F2], the plane through $A,B,C$ has value $1+\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4$ at $D$, while $D$'s lifted height is $1+\varepsilon^8$. Their difference is $\varepsilon^8-\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^4$, whose least nonzero exponent is $1$ with coefficient $-1$. Thus $D$ lies formally below the plane through $A,B,C$, and diagonal $AC$ is illegal. The flip selects $BD$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The plane through $A,B,D$ has value $2+\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^8-\varepsilon$ at $C$; subtracting from $C$'s height $2+\varepsilon^4$ gives $\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4-\varepsilon^8$, which is formally positive. The plane through $B,C,D$ has value $\varepsilon^8-\varepsilon^4+\varepsilon^2$ at $A$; subtracting from $A$'s height $\varepsilon$ gives $\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon^4-\varepsilon^8$, also formally positive. Hence both $ABD$ and $BCD$ are lower triangles for the common lift. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 When three synthetic identifiers are inserted below $1,2,3,4$, each input rank increases by three and each exponent $2^{r_i}$ is multiplied by $8$. Thus every input-only determinant polynomial becomes the four-site polynomial with $\varepsilon$ replaced by $\varepsilon^8$, which preserves the first nonzero coefficient sign. The augmented run therefore retains diagonal $BD$, and [F5] returns the stated weakly empty triangulation. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $n\ge4$ weighted sites of projected affine dimension three, the number of 3D Delaunay tetrahedra or weighted regular tetrahedra returned by the fixed formal lift is at most $n(n-3)/2$, hence $O(n^2)$. No planar $O(n)$ bound or mesh-quality guarantee is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite indexed weighted site set of projected affine dimension three and the fixed-universe formal lift.

[F1] [[def-three-dimensional-delaunay-and-weighted-regular-lower-hull]]: lower facets project to regular cells; zero weights give ordinary Delaunay tetrahedra.

[F2] [[thm-lexicographic-lift-tie-break-consistent]]: any five lifted sites whose projected base contains four affinely independent sites have a nonzero formal determinant.

[F3] [[lem-simplicial-four-polytope-facet-count]]: every full-dimensional convex 4-polytope with $m\ge5$ vertices has at most $m(m-3)/2$ facets.

[F4] [[thm-three-dimensional-lower-hull-coverage-empty-sphere-and-termination]]: the returned tetrahedra are exactly the full-dimensional lower simplices of the formal lift.

[A1] The projected site set has affine dimension three.

## Proof

1.1 Assume $n\ge5$. For each five-site tuple whose projected points contain four affinely independent sites, order four such sites first and the fifth last, and let $P(\varepsilon)$ be its lifted determinant polynomial. By [F2], this polynomial is nonzero. Write it as $c\varepsilon^k+\sum_j c_j\varepsilon^{k_j}$, where $c\ne0$ and every $k_j>k$. If $C=\sum_j|c_j|>0$, then for $0<\varepsilon<\min(1,|c|/(2C))$, the absolute value of the higher terms after dividing by $\varepsilon^k$ is at most $C\varepsilon<|c|/2$, since each $k_j-k$ is a positive integer; if $C=0$, its sign is constant for every $\varepsilon>0$. Thus each such determinant has its formal sign for all sufficiently small positive real $\varepsilon$. There are finitely many relevant tuples, so choose one positive real $\varepsilon$ small enough for all of them. Use this same value to evaluate the heights of every site. By [F4], each output tetrahedron is a lower simplex of the formal lift. On its affinely independent projected base, every other site's formal support determinant is nonzero by [F2]; the preceding sign specialization preserves its sign. If $O$ is the projected orientation determinant of the base, $h_q$ is the query height, and $\ell(q)$ is the height of the base graph plane at the query, row subtraction gives the displayed-order identity $P=-O(h_q-\ell(q))$. As $O\ne0$ and is unchanged by height specialization, the same four real lifted points support a real lower facet and every other lifted point lies strictly above it. No fifth point is in that facet. Distinct output tetrahedra therefore correspond to distinct facets of this one real convex hull. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]


2.1 If $n=4$, at most one four-site candidate is output, and $1\le4(4-3)/2$. If $n\ge5$, choose four affinely independent projected sites and a fifth distinct site. Their formal determinant is nonzero by [F2], and its real specialization at the common value from step 1.1 is nonzero. Hence the real lifted convex hull is full-dimensional in $\mathbb R^4$. Let $m\le n$ be its number of extreme vertices; full dimension forces $m\ge5$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]


3.1 Apply [F3] to this full-dimensional convex 4-polytope. Its total number of facets, hence also its number of lower facets, is at most $m(m-3)/2$. By step 1.1, the output tetrahedra inject into those facets. The function $s(s-3)/2$ is increasing for integers $s\ge5$, so the output count is at most $n(n-3)/2$. This is quadratic; the argument establishes no angle or tetrahedral-quality bound. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Whenever [[alg-certified-integer-order-bessel-evaluation]] returns `success`,
its interval contains the requested $J_n(x)$ or scaled modified Bessel value
$e^{-x}I_n(x)$ and passes the requested absolute-radius test. A relative
certificate is valid only when zero is outside the interval and the relative
test passes. The theorem makes no success guarantee for every input or finite
cap. Every execution with finite caps terminates.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A successful return of
[[alg-certified-integer-order-bessel-evaluation]] with a sound outward interval
backend.

[A1] [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] supplies the finite real
sine, cosine, and exponential ranges used by the midpoint branches; every
finite range is sound by [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]].

[A2] [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] and
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]: every finite
interval operation encloses its exact result.

[F1] [[alg-certified-integer-order-bessel-evaluation]]: series, midpoint,
and finite Miller candidates are returned only after their respective tail or
terminal-error enclosures are applied; its exact scaled-$I$ input $x=0$
branch returns the corresponding defining-series value. Candidate
intersections are taken only when nonempty.

[F2] [[def-integer-order-bessel-series]] and
[[def-real-elementary-functions-and-domains]]: at $x=0$, the defining series
gives $I_0(0)=1$, $I_n(0)=0$ for $n\ge1$, and $e^0=1$.

[F3] [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]: success requires exact
inclusion and the stated radius; relative certification requires zero
exclusion.

[F4] [[lem-integer-order-bessel-series-tail]]: the truncated $J_n$ series
tail is enclosed by the geometric bound when its ratio test passes.

[F5] [[lem-finite-miller-terminal-error-identity]]: the finite normalized
backward recurrence error is exactly the displayed terminal-contamination
expression whenever its denominators are nonzero.

[F6] [[lem-bessel-integral-midpoint-error]]: the midpoint $J_n$ enclosure
contains the exact cosine integral.

[F7] [[lem-scaled-modified-bessel-midpoint-error]]: the midpoint enclosure
contains the exact scaled $I_n$ integral.

[F8] [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]: its
Machin identity and finite arctangent tails enclose $\pi$ for the midpoint
mesh; the elementary-range calls are sound by [A1].

## Proof
1.1 If the target is scaled $I$ and $x=0$, the defining series [F2] gives
$e^{-x}I_n(x)=1$ for $n=0$ and $0$ for $n\ge1$, so the exact internal singleton contains the target; its final outward conversion also contains it by [A2], and the algorithm tests the actual rounded radius. Otherwise, the power-series candidate contains
$J_n(x)$ by [F4]. The two midpoint candidates contain their integrals by [F6]
and [F7]; their finite sine, cosine, and exponential ranges are sound by
[A1], their mesh constant is enclosed by [F8], and their arithmetic interval
operations are sound by [A2]. The Miller candidate contains $J_n(x)$ because
its interval evaluates the exact error expression in [F5] and subtracts that
interval from the normalized backward value, using sound interval operations
[A2]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8]

2.1 Every candidate used by the procedure therefore contains the same exact requested value. Any nonempty intersection of candidates also contains that value. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 The algorithm reports success only after the containing interval passes the absolute-radius test and, when reported, the zero-excluding relative test in [F3]. Otherwise it returns an inconclusive or range status under finite caps. Thus the success claims are sound and do not rely on a limit as the Miller terminal index grows. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 The stage and candidate loops are finite, every series and recurrence uses at most its stated finite index, and each elementary-range call has a finite DAG, format, and truncation index. Hence every capped execution terminates. [given, A1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

For $\gamma=7/5$, take left primitive data $(\rho_L,u_L,p_L)=(1,0,1)$ and
right data $(\rho_R,u_R,p_R)=(1/8,0,1/10)$. Set
$E_K=p_K/(\gamma-1)+\rho_Ku_K^2/2$ and
$U_K=(\rho_K,\rho_Ku_K,E_K)$ for $K=L,R$; both conserved states lie in
$\mathcal G_\gamma$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Sod initial states, the ideal-gas pressure response, its root/vacuum criterion, and the finite-budget bracket solver.

[F1] [[def-ideal-gas-euler-state-and-pressure]]: $\rho>0,p>0$ is equivalent to the declared admissible-state inequalities for the ideal-gas model.

[F2] [[def-euler-star-pressure-response]]: $\Phi(p)=f_L(p)+f_R(p)+u_R-u_L$ with rarefaction response below $p_K$ and shock response above it.

[F3] [[thm-euler-star-pressure-root-and-vacuum-criterion]]: $\Phi(0+)<0$ gives a unique positive root; $\Phi$ is strictly increasing.

[F4] [[lem-euler-pressure-solver-bracket-and-termination]]: for a budget $N$ with $(3/4)^N P\le\tau$, the safeguarded procedure returns a bracket of width at most $\tau$ containing that root.

## Verification

1.1 The densities and pressures are positive, so [F1] gives admissible states. The sound speeds are $c_L=\sqrt{7/5}$ and $c_R=\sqrt{28/25}$. Since both velocities are zero, $\Phi(0+)=-2(c_L+c_R)/(\gamma-1)<0$. By [F3] there is one positive star pressure $p_*$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 At $p=1/10=p_R$, $f_R(p)=0$ while $p<p_L$ makes the left rarefaction response strictly negative; hence $\Phi(1/10)<0$. At $p=1=p_L$, $f_L(p)=0$ while $p>p_R$ makes the right shock response strictly positive; hence $\Phi(1)>0$. Strict increase gives $1/10<p_*<1$, so the left wave is a rarefaction and the right wave is a shock. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 The contact between the two acoustic waves has pressure $p_*$ and common velocity $u_*=u_L-f_L(p_*)=u_R+f_R(p_*)$. Equality follows by rearranging $\Phi(p_*)=0$. The explicit theorem bracket $[0,P]$ and [F4] give a finite-budget enclosure of any prescribed positive width when the budget meets its bound; insufficient budgets return `budget-exhausted` with the root still bracketed. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. On the unit reference triangle, the affine function $v(x,y)=x$ gives a finite witness that the symmetric form contains an extra adjoint-consistency term: $a_h^1(v,v)-a_h^0(v,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega}v\partial_nv=-1/2$. In the duality calculation for an error $e$ and a zero-trace adjoint solution $\zeta_e$, that same term cancels the boundary flux in the symmetric $L^2$ identity. It is absent from the nonsymmetric form, which leaves the separate pairing $\int_{\partial\Omega}e\partial_n\zeta_e$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the unit triangle; $v=x$; the symmetric and nonsymmetric forms of [[def-nitsche-boundary-penalty-forms]]; and an error/adjoint pair in the hypotheses of both L2 theorems, including their stated regularity assumptions.

[F1] On the diagonal, $a_h^1(v,v)-a_h^0(v,v)=-\sum_F\int_Fv\partial_nv$ by the two form definitions ([[def-nitsche-boundary-penalty-forms]]).

[F2] A function in $H^1_0(\Omega)$ has zero boundary-facet trace ([[lem-nitsche-h-one-zero-functions-have-zero-facet-traces]]).

[F3] Under the exact and adjoint regularity/PDE hypotheses stated in the two L2 theorems, the fractional weak Green supplier proves their Green identities and interior flux cancellation ([[lem-nitsche-fractional-weak-green-and-flux-cancellation]]).

## Verification

**Given:** The finite triangle calculation and the duality setup in [F3].

1.1 The triangle has edges $y=0$, $x=0$, and $x+y=1$. On the first edge $\partial_nv=0$; on the second $v=0$; on the diagonal $n=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, $\partial_nv=1/\sqrt2$, and the arclength parametrization $(t,1-t)$ has $ds=\sqrt2\,dt$. Therefore $\sum_F\int_Fv\partial_nv=\int_0^1t\,dt=1/2$. Substitution in [F1] gives the asserted finite difference $-1/2$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For the adjoint Poisson equation, [F3] gives $\|e\|_2^2=\int_\Omega\nabla e\cdot\nabla\zeta_e-\sum_F\int_Fe\partial_n\zeta_e$. The symmetric form contains the transposed term $-\sum_F\int_Fe\partial_n\zeta_e$; after subtracting the zero-trace discrete test, the remaining flux is paired with the adjoint interpolation error. The nonsymmetric form has no transposed consistency term; its zero-trace discrete tests satisfy $a_h^0(e,z_h)=\int_\Omega\nabla e\cdot\nabla z_h$, leaving the full pairing $-\sum_F\int_Fe\partial_n\zeta_e$ in the error identity. Thus the symmetric method reduces the adjoint boundary defect to an approximation residual, while the nonsymmetric method retains it. The zero boundary traces used here follow from [F2], and the two $L^2$ theorem items retain their distinct hypotheses and rates. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, the mini-element hypotheses of [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, and an initial value $u_h^0\in Z_h$. On every finite positive time partition there is at least one mixed solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=1}^N$ of the backward Euler scheme. Every such solution satisfies, for $0\le m\le N$, the work-form inequality
$$\frac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+\nu\sum_{n=1}^m\tau_n\|\nabla u_h^n\|_2^2\le\frac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\sum_{n=1}^m\tau_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$$
Consequently it satisfies the mesh-independent estimate
$$\frac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+\frac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+\frac{\nu}{2}\sum_{n=1}^m\tau_n\|\nabla u_h^n\|_2^2\le\frac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\frac{C_P(D)^2}{2\nu}\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2)}^2.$$
The constant is independent of mesh size and time-step sizes.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the MINI spaces, $\nu>0$, a finite partition, $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2)$, and $u_h^0\in Z_h$.

[A1] Countable Choice is inherited from the MINI/Stokes stability supplier; no arbitrary-index choice is used inside a single finite partition. ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-na-mini-element-fortin-stability]])

[F1] The velocity mass form is real Hilbert; $a_\nu(z,z)=2\nu\|\varepsilon(z)\|_2^2\ge\nu\|\nabla z\|_2^2$ on $H^1_0$. ([[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-korn-identity]])

[F2] $c(z;z,z)=0$ for every $z\in V$, and $c$ is continuous on the finite-dimensional MINI space. ([[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]], [[lem-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form-bound]])

[F3] A continuous finite-dimensional map with positive outward radial pairing on a sphere has a zero in the ball. ([[lem-pe12-outward-zero-brouwer]])

[F4] The stable MINI pair has a positive discrete inf-sup constant, so the pressure map is injective and the velocity constraint map is onto. ([[thm-na-mini-element-fortin-stability]], [[def-na-discrete-weak-and-exact-divergence-free-spaces]])

[F5] The identity $2(x-y,x)=\|x\|^2-\|y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2$ holds in $L^2$, and Poincare gives $\|z\|_2\le C_P(D)\|\nabla z\|_2$. ([[lem-parabolic-discrete-energy-identity]], [[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]])

[F6] Holder and Young absorb $\|f_h^n\|_2\|u_h^n\|_2$ into $\nu\|\nabla u_h^n\|_2^2/2$ with remainder $C_P(D)^2\|f_h^n\|_2^2/(2\nu)$. ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]], [[thm-young-inequality-real-exponents]])

[F7] The norm of a Bochner integral is at most the integral of the norm. ([[lem-bochner-integral-norm-inequality]])

## Proof

1.1 Fix a time cell and the previous value $u_h^{n-1}\in Z_h$. On $Z_h$, define $F_n(z)\in Z_h^*$ by $\langle F_n(z),w_h\rangle=\tau_n^{-1}(z-u_h^{n-1},w_h)_{L^2}+a_\nu(z,w_h)+c(z;z,w_h)-(f_h^n,w_h)_{L^2}.$ The map is continuous by [F2] and finite dimensionality. If $Z_h=\{0\}$ its only velocity is zero; otherwise represent $F_n$ in coordinates of a gradient-orthonormal basis of $Z_h$. [A1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 By [F1]–[F2], $\langle F_n(z),z\rangle\ge\nu\|\nabla z\|_2^2-C_P(D)\big(\tau_n^{-1}\|u_h^{n-1}\|_2+\|f_h^n\|_2\big)\|\nabla z\|_2.$ Choose $R$ so the right side is strictly positive whenever $\|\nabla z\|_2=R$. The outward-zero result [F3] supplies $u_h^n\in Z_h$ with $F_n(u_h^n)=0$. [F1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $G_n(v_h)$ be the velocity residual (time term plus viscosity and convection minus forcing). Step 2.1 gives $G_n=0$ on $Z_h=\ker\mathcal B$, where $\mathcal Bv_h(q_h)=b(v_h,q_h)$. Since [F4] makes $\mathcal B$ onto $Q_h^*$, $\mathcal B^*$ is injective and its range is contained in $(\ker\mathcal B)^\circ$. Rank-nullity gives both spaces dimension $\dim Q_h$, so they are equal. Thus $-G_n=\mathcal B^*p_h^n$ for a unique $p_h^n\in Q_h$, which gives the stated mixed equation with the correct residual sign. Repeating the finite step for $n=1,\ldots,N$ gives a mixed solution. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Test the mixed equation with $u_h^n$. Its pressure term is zero since $u_h^n\in Z_h$, and its convective term is zero by [F2]. Apply [F5] to the time term and [F1] to the viscosity term, obtaining $\frac12(\|u_h^n\|_2^2-\|u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2)+\nu\tau_n\|\nabla u_h^n\|_2^2\le\tau_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$ The right side is retained with its sign; it follows directly from the tested equation, skew cancellation, and the lower Korn bound. ## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as required by the Fourier-space and interpolation suppliers. Fix $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, $a>0$, and let $\Omega=(0,1)^d$. The smooth graph $\{(x,f(x)):x\in\overline\Omega\}$ with $f(x)=e^{-\pi|x|^2}$ is interpolated from midpoint-grid samples by the normalized Matérn kernel of smoothness $\nu$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, Countable Choice, the fixed $d,\nu,a$, the cube, the function $f$, and midpoint grids
$$X_m=\left\{\left(\frac{i_1+1/2}{m},\ldots,\frac{i_d+1/2}{m}\right):0\le i_j<m\right\},\qquad m\in\mathbb N,\quad m\ge1.$$

[F1] An admitted domain is nonempty, bounded and Lipschitz and has a single cone radius and aperture at every point of the closure; the fill distance is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{y\in X}|x-y|$. ([[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]])

[F2] Every Schwartz function is in the Fourier Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $s>d/2$, and $H^s(\Omega)$ consists of restrictions of whole-space members. ([[lem-schwartz-dense-in-fourier-bessel-potential-space]], [[def-bessel-potential-space-and-restriction-quotient]])

[F3] The real exponential is smooth with derivative itself; repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules show every partial derivative of $f$ is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of $e^{-\pi|x|^2}$. ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F4] The Schwartz seminorms require polynomially weighted derivatives to be bounded. For any degree $M\ge0$, take an integer $n\ge1$ with $2n\ge M$; for $r\ge1$, $r^M\le r^{2n}$ and exponential domination applied with $x=r^2$ gives $r^{2n}e^{-\pi r^2}\to0$. On $|x|\le1$, each polynomial is bounded by the sum of the absolute values of its finitely many coefficients. ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]])

[F5] The Matérn interpolation error and power function are bounded by $C h_X^\nu$ on an admitted cone domain for small fill distance. ([[thm-matern-interpolation-fill-distance-error]])



**Proof technique:** verify the domain, regularity, and grid radius, then apply the fill-distance theorem.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** verify the domain, regularity, and grid radius, then apply the fill-distance theorem.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 The cube is bounded and Lipschitz. At a boundary point $p$, let $I$ be the nonempty set of active coordinates ($p_j=0$ or $1$), with inward signs $\sigma_j=1$ at $0$ and $-1$ at $1$. Put $u_j=\sigma_j/\sqrt{|I|}$ for $j\in I$ and $u_j=0$ otherwise. In the orthogonal coordinates $x=p+y+tu$ with $y\perp u$, a sufficiently small neighborhood has no constraints from inactive coordinates, and the active inequalities reduce to $$t>\max_{j\in I}(-\sqrt{|I|}\,\sigma_j y_j).$$ This is the epigraph of a finite maximum of linear functions, hence a local Lipschitz graph with the cube on one side. The cube also satisfies the uniform cone condition: for $x\in[0,1]^d$, let $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $\sigma_j=-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ let $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence for every coordinate, $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The sites in $X_m$ are distinct. Each $x\in(0,1)^d$ is at coordinatewise distance at most $1/(2m)$ from a midpoint in each grid interval, so $h_{X_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$. By [F3], every partial derivative of $f$ is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of $e^{-\pi|x|^2}$; [F4] makes every polynomially weighted derivative bounded, so $f$ is Schwartz. Then [F2] gives $f|_\Omega\in H^s(\Omega)$ for $s=\nu+d/2$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For all sufficiently large $m$, step 2.1 gives $h_{X_m}\le h_0$ from [F5]. The Matérn interpolation theorem therefore yields $$\|f-s_{X_m}f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le C h_{X_m}^\nu\|f\|_{H^s(\Omega)}\le C\left(\frac{\sqrt d}{2m}\right)^\nu\|f\|_{H^s(\Omega)},\qquad \sup_{x\in\Omega}P_{X_m}(x)\le C\left(\frac{\sqrt d}{2m}\right)^\nu.$$ The graph samples are the scattered surface data, and the bound uses fill distance alone; no mesh-ratio condition is needed. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as required by the Fourier-space and interpolation suppliers. Fix $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, $a>0$, and let $\Omega=(0,1)^d$. The smooth graph $\{(x,f(x)):x\in\overline\Omega\}$ with $f(x)=e^{-\pi|x|^2}$ is interpolated from midpoint-grid samples by the normalized Matérn kernel of smoothness $\nu$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, Countable Choice, the fixed $d,\nu,a$, the cube, the function $f$, and midpoint grids
$$X_m=\left\{\left(\frac{i_1+1/2}{m},\ldots,\frac{i_d+1/2}{m}\right):0\le i_j<m\right\},\qquad m\in\mathbb N,\quad m\ge1.$$

[F1] An admitted domain is nonempty, bounded and Lipschitz and has a single cone radius and aperture at every point of the closure; the fill distance is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{y\in X}|x-y|$. ([[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]])

[F2] Every Schwartz function is in the Fourier Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $s>d/2$, and $H^s(\Omega)$ consists of restrictions of whole-space members. ([[lem-schwartz-dense-in-fourier-bessel-potential-space]], [[def-bessel-potential-space-and-restriction-quotient]])

[F3] The real exponential is smooth with derivative itself; repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules show every partial derivative of $f$ is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of $e^{-\pi|x|^2}$. ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F4] The Schwartz seminorms require polynomially weighted derivatives to be bounded. For any degree $M\ge0$, take an integer $n\ge1$ with $2n\ge M$; for $r\ge1$, $r^M\le r^{2n}$ and exponential domination applied with $x=r^2$ gives $r^{2n}e^{-\pi r^2}\to0$. On $|x|\le1$, each polynomial is bounded by the sum of the absolute values of its finitely many coefficients. ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]])

[F5] The Matérn interpolation error and power function are bounded by $C h_X^\nu$ on an admitted cone domain for small fill distance. ([[thm-matern-interpolation-fill-distance-error]])



**Proof technique:** verify the domain, regularity, and grid radius, then apply the fill-distance theorem.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** verify the domain, regularity, and grid radius, then apply the fill-distance theorem.

**Given:** The data above.

1.1 The cube is bounded and Lipschitz. At a boundary point $p$, let $I$ be the nonempty set of active coordinates ($p_j=0$ or $1$), with inward signs $\sigma_j=1$ at $0$ and $-1$ at $1$. Put $u_j=\sigma_j/\sqrt{|I|}$ for $j\in I$ and $u_j=0$ otherwise. In the orthogonal coordinates $x=p+y+tu$ with $y\perp u$, a sufficiently small neighborhood has no constraints from inactive coordinates, and the active inequalities reduce to $$t>\max_{j\in I}(-\sqrt{|I|}\,\sigma_j y_j).$$ This is the epigraph of a finite maximum of linear functions, hence a local Lipschitz graph with the cube on one side. The cube also satisfies the uniform cone condition: for $x\in[0,1]^d$, let $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $\sigma_j=-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ let $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence for every coordinate, $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The sites in $X_m$ are distinct. Each $x\in(0,1)^d$ is at coordinatewise distance at most $1/(2m)$ from a midpoint in each grid interval, so $h_{X_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$. By [F3], every partial derivative of $f$ is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of $e^{-\pi|x|^2}$; [F4] makes every polynomially weighted derivative bounded, so $f$ is Schwartz. Then [F2] gives $f|_\Omega\in H^s(\Omega)$ for $s=\nu+d/2$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For all sufficiently large $m$, step 2.1 gives $h_{X_m}\le h_0$ from [F5]. The Matérn interpolation theorem therefore yields $$\|f-s_{X_m}f\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le C h_{X_m}^\nu\|f\|_{H^s(\Omega)}\le C\left(\frac{\sqrt d}{2m}\right)^\nu\|f\|_{H^s(\Omega)},\qquad \sup_{x\in\Omega}P_{X_m}(x)\le C\left(\frac{\sqrt d}{2m}\right)^\nu.$$ The graph samples are the scattered surface data, and the bound uses fill distance alone; no mesh-ratio condition is needed. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, the Darcy data in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]], and a facet-connected shape-regular mesh. For at least two cells, set $C_R$ as in the stable lift theorem and define
$$\widehat\beta=(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2},\quad M_a=\kappa_{\min}^{-1},\quad M_b=1,\quad\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}.$$
Let $(u,p)$ solve the continuous source-only Darcy problem ($F=0$) and $(u_h,p_h)$ the RT0/P0 Galerkin system. For any $w_h\in V_h,r_h\in Q_h$, put $\delta_u=\|u-w_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$, $\delta_p=\|p-r_h\|_2$, and
$$R_h=\widehat\beta^{-1}M_b\delta_u,$$
$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\widehat\beta^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$
Then the discrete pair exists uniquely and
$$\|u-u_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le U_h,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_2\le P_h,\qquad \|u-u_h\|_{K^{-1}}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1/2}U_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh $V_h=Q_h=\{0\}$, so the unique discrete pair is $(0,0)$; the nonzero-$Q_h$ error theorem is not invoked. The constants display permeability contrast and do not assert contrast-independent robustness.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a continuous source-only Darcy solution, a facet-connected shape-regular mesh, and the stated permeability bounds.

[A1] Countable Choice is required by the continuous mixed and Galerkin solvability suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The continuous Darcy pair exists uniquely in $V\times Q$. ([[thm-na-darcy-mixed-wellposedness]])

[F2] For nonzero $Q_h$, the stable lift gives $\beta_h\ge\widehat\beta>0$. ([[thm-na-rt0-p0-bounded-divergence-lift-and-infsup]])

[F3] The discrete mixed kernel is exactly divergencefree. ([[lem-na-rt0-p0-kernel-is-divergencefree]])

[F4] The Darcy form obeys $|a(v,w)|\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\|w\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$ and $|b(v,q)|\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\|q\|_2$; on the divergencefree kernel, $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}^2$. ([[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]])

[F5] For conforming finite-dimensional subspaces, nonzero $Q_h$, positive $\beta_h$, and discrete-kernel coercivity, the actual mixed Galerkin solution is unique and satisfies the displayed explicit $U_h,P_h$ bound with $\beta_h$ retained. ([[thm-na-mixed-galerkin-quasioptimality]])

[F6] A one-cell RT0 field with zero flux on every facet is zero, by facet-flux unisolvence; a one-cell mean-zero P0 space is zero. ([[lem-na-rt0-unisolvence-and-global-conformity]], [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]])

## Proof

1.1 Suppose first there are at least two cells. Facet-connectedness implies there are at least two independent cell constants before imposing the one mean constraint, hence $Q_h\ne\{0\}$. The stable lift [F2] gives a positive discrete inf-sup constant. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, the Darcy data in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]], and a facet-connected shape-regular mesh. For at least two cells, set $C_R$ as in the stable lift theorem and define
$$\widehat\beta=(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2},\quad M_a=\kappa_{\min}^{-1},\quad M_b=1,\quad\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}.$$
Let $(u,p)$ solve the continuous source-only Darcy problem ($F=0$) and $(u_h,p_h)$ the RT0/P0 Galerkin system. For any $w_h\in V_h,r_h\in Q_h$, put $\delta_u=\|u-w_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$, $\delta_p=\|p-r_h\|_2$, and
$$R_h=\widehat\beta^{-1}M_b\delta_u,$$
$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\widehat\beta^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$
Then the discrete pair exists uniquely and
$$\|u-u_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le U_h,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_2\le P_h,\qquad \|u-u_h\|_{K^{-1}}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1/2}U_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh $V_h=Q_h=\{0\}$, so the unique discrete pair is $(0,0)$; the nonzero-$Q_h$ error theorem is not invoked. The constants display permeability contrast and do not assert contrast-independent robustness.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, a continuous source-only Darcy solution, a facet-connected shape-regular mesh, and the stated permeability bounds.

[A1] Countable Choice is required by the continuous mixed and Galerkin solvability suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] The continuous Darcy pair exists uniquely in $V\times Q$. ([[thm-na-darcy-mixed-wellposedness]])

[F2] For nonzero $Q_h$, the stable lift gives $\beta_h\ge\widehat\beta>0$. ([[thm-na-rt0-p0-bounded-divergence-lift-and-infsup]])

[F3] The discrete mixed kernel is exactly divergencefree. ([[lem-na-rt0-p0-kernel-is-divergencefree]])

[F4] The Darcy form obeys $|a(v,w)|\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\|w\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$ and $|b(v,q)|\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\|q\|_2$; on the divergencefree kernel, $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}^2$. ([[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]])

[F5] For conforming finite-dimensional subspaces, nonzero $Q_h$, positive $\beta_h$, and discrete-kernel coercivity, the actual mixed Galerkin solution is unique and satisfies the displayed explicit $U_h,P_h$ bound with $\beta_h$ retained. ([[thm-na-mixed-galerkin-quasioptimality]])

[F6] A one-cell RT0 field with zero flux on every facet is zero, by facet-flux unisolvence; a one-cell mean-zero P0 space is zero. ([[lem-na-rt0-unisolvence-and-global-conformity]], [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]])

## Proof

1.1 Suppose first there are at least two cells. Facet-connectedness implies there are at least two independent cell constants before imposing the one mean constraint, hence $Q_h\ne\{0\}$. The stable lift [F2] gives a positive discrete inf-sup constant. If $z_h$ belongs to the discrete kernel, [F3] gives $\operatorname{div}z_h=0$; hence its graph norm is its $L^2$ norm and the coefficient lower bound [F4] gives discrete coercivity with $\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$. The bounds in [F4] give $M_a=\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$ and $M_b=1$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Apply [F5] to the conforming spaces $V_h\subset V$, $Q_h\subset Q$, continuous solution [F1], and the constants in step 1.1. This gives a unique Galerkin pair and the bound with $\beta_h$. Since $\beta_h\ge\widehat\beta$, each occurrence of $\beta_h^{-1}$ in the supplied formulas is no larger than $\widehat\beta^{-1}$; all coefficients and best-approximation errors are nonnegative, so replacing $\beta_h^{-1}$ by $\widehat\beta^{-1}$ only enlarges $R_h,U_h,P_h$. The $L^2$ flux error estimate follows from $\|e\|_{K^{-1}}^2\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|e\|_2^2$. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If the mesh has one cell, every facet is a physical-boundary facet. The boundary-zero facet moments and [F6] force $V_h=\{0\}$, while a constant with zero global mean is zero, so $Q_h=\{0\}$. The zero pair is the sole discrete pair. Finally $M_a/\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}/\kappa_{\min}$, making the permeability-contrast dependence explicit in the formulas rather than uniform in that ratio. [F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra, cases] ∎

## Example

Let $D=(0,1)^3$, $f=0$, and choose a nonzero $\chi\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$, for example a smooth bump supported in $(1/4,3/4)$. Put $\psi(x,y,z)=\chi(x)\chi(y)\chi(z)$ and
$$u_0=(\partial_y\psi,-\partial_x\psi,0).$$
This supplies explicit smooth no-slip data for a three-dimensional MINI backward Euler computation; initialize the discrete scheme with $u_h^0=P_{Z_h}u_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $\nu>0$, the unit cube, the displayed compactly supported initial field, zero forcing, and any shape-regular matching mesh and finite time partition.

[F1] The L2 orthogonal projector $P_{Z_h}$ exists, and the MINI backward Euler equations have a solution and every solution satisfies the discrete energy inequality. ([[thm-na-discrete-helmholtz-projection-and-pressure-schur]], [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], [[thm-na-mini-be-step-existence-energy]])

[F2] In three dimensions the uniqueness result is conditional on a strong solution branch with the regularity and equation hypotheses stated there. ([[thm-na-ns-weak-solution-uniqueness-2d-and-weak-strong-3d]])

[F3] $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of compactly supported smooth fields. ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]])

## Verification

1.1 The field $u_0$ is smooth and compactly supported in $D$, so it belongs to $H^1_0(D)^3$. Its divergence is $\partial_x\partial_y\psi-\partial_y\partial_x\psi=\chi'(x)\chi'(y)\chi(z)-\chi'(x)\chi'(y)\chi(z)=0,$ by direct product differentiation. Thus $u_0\in V_\sigma$ and has zero boundary trace. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 For any mesh and finite partition, [F1] supplies a discrete trajectory; with $f=0$, its kinetic energy, time jumps and accumulated viscous dissipation obey the budget in [[ex-na-mini-backward-euler-energy-budget]]. If the continuum data admit a strong branch satisfying [F2], the comparison theorem makes that branch unique among energy weak solutions on its interval. Without that additional strong-solution hypothesis, neither the scheme's existence nor its energy budget selects a unique three-dimensional weak trajectory or asserts that the computed flow is turbulent. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
